responsibilities.role: Director of Nursing/Health Care Practitioner Supervisor
responsibilities.duty: Protects clients immediately when a report involves client safety, and supports clinical record review.
Submit only accurate, supported claims, take part in audits, and report suspected errors.
Report suspected misconduct promptly, cooperate with investigations and complete compliance training.

documentation: Governing body minutes appointing the compliance officer
Compliance report log and investigation files
Findings, corrective action plans and verification of completion
Copies of reports to outside agencies and proof of submission
Billing integrity audit reports and refund records
Annual financial statement and any audit or CPA review filed with the Division
Training attendance records (orientation and annual in-service)
Quarterly compliance reports to the governing body

policies.title: Whistleblower Protection
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, compliance officer, supervisors, and all employees and contractors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect any person who reports in good faith unethical, fraudulent or illegal activity from retaliation, and to give staff a confidential channel to report.
policies.policy:
This policy meets Best Practices §IV, Corporate Compliance Policy 6 – Protection for those reporting unethical, fraudulent or illegal activity ("whistle-blower" protection).

[AGENCY NAME] prohibits retaliation against any employee or other person who reports in good faith, or takes part in an investigation of, a suspected violation of law or regulation, fraud, abuse, a client-safety concern, or an unethical practice. This includes reports made inside the agency or to any government agency, and a refusal to take part in an unlawful act, such as performing a task that has not been delegated by the health care practitioner supervisor (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). It also includes the right to take action under the federal False Claims Act, which protects employees from retaliation for lawful acts in furtherance of a False Claims Act action (31 USC 3730(h)).

The agency provides a confidential reporting channel and, where possible, keeps the reporter's identity confidential. Anonymous reports are accepted. Retaliation is itself misconduct and leads to discipline up to and including termination. This policy is covered in orientation and in the corporate compliance in-service.

definitions.definition: A person who reports, or takes part in an investigation of, suspected unethical, fraudulent or illegal activity.
Any adverse action taken because of a protected report, such as discharge, demotion, reduced hours or assignments, discipline, harassment, threats, intimidation or blacklisting.
A reasonable belief that the information reported is true. A report made in good faith is protected even if the concern is not substantiated.
A method to report, by telephone, email, mail or in person, that limits disclosure of the reporter's identity to those who need it to investigate.

procedures: The compliance officer publishes the confidential reporting channel: telephone [PHONE], email [EMAIL], and mailing address [ADDRESS], and posts it where staff meet and in the employee handbook. Anonymous reports are accepted.

At orientation (PER-06), human resources reviews this policy with every new employee, explains that retaliation is prohibited, and obtains a signed acknowledgment, which is filed in the personnel record (PER-04).
The compliance officer includes whistleblower protection in the annual corporate compliance in-service (PER-07) and records attendance.

Anyone who receives a report logs it the same day under the compliance report log in ADM-06 and notifies the compliance officer. The reporter's identity is shared only with those who need to know to investigate or protect a client.
The compliance officer acknowledges the report to the reporter (if known) within 2 business days and tells the reporter that retaliation is prohibited and whom to contact if it occurs.
The compliance officer reviews every report and investigates under ADM-06. Persons named in the report do not take part in the investigation or in any decision about the reporter.

The compliance officer follows up with the reporter at 30 days and again when the matter is closed, to say what can be shared about the outcome and to ask about any retaliation. Each contact is documented.

Before any adverse action (discipline, schedule reduction, reassignment, termination) is taken against an employee who has made a report in the past 12 months, the Administrator and human resources review the proposed action and confirm in writing that it is unrelated to the report.

An employee who believes they have faced retaliation reports it to the compliance officer or the Administrator, or if either is the subject of the complaint, to the governing body chair. The complaint is investigated within 30 days.

If retaliation is substantiated, the Administrator takes corrective action at once, which may include reinstatement, restoration of hours or assignments, and discipline of the responsible person, up to and including termination. The action is documented.
The compliance officer reports the number of whistleblower reports and any retaliation findings to the governing body at least quarterly, without identifying reporters.

Staff are told that they may also report directly to government agencies, such as the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs or NJ Board of Nursing, without first reporting to the agency, and the agency will not interfere with that right.
All whistleblower records are stored in a restricted-access file apart from the personnel record and are kept for at least [RETENTION PERIOD, not less than 6 years].

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and hears complaints of retaliation involving the Administrator or compliance officer.
Ensures no retaliation occurs, reviews proposed adverse actions against reporters, and takes corrective action.
Runs the confidential channel, protects reporter identity, follows up with reporters and reports to the governing body.
Pass on any report received at once and never retaliate or allow others to do so.
Delivers orientation on this policy, files acknowledgments and screens adverse actions.
Report concerns in good faith and cooperate with investigations.

documentation: Signed whistleblower policy acknowledgments in personnel records
Compliance report log entries and confidential investigation files
Records of follow-up contacts with reporters
Pre-action review forms for adverse actions against reporters
Orientation and in-service attendance records
Quarterly compliance report to the governing body

policies.title: Assignment by Level of Care; NJ Certification Required
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Director of Nursing/Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, scheduling and intake staff, human resources, and all clinical and aide staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every person assigned to a client is authorized to provide the required service at the level of care in the plan of care, that Certified Nurse Assistants and unlicensed assistive personnel are not assigned to in-home personal care, and that every licensed or certified staff member shows proof of current New Jersey licensure or certification.
policies.policy:
This policy meets Best Practices §IV, Corporate Compliance Policy 1 and Best Practices §IV, Corporate Compliance Policy 2.

Corporate Compliance Policy 1 – Assignment for the appropriate level of care: [AGENCY NAME] assigns only individuals who are authorized to provide the required service, and the assignment must match the level of care written in the client's plan of care. Hands-on personal care in the home is assigned only to an actively certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide (CHHA) employed by the agency, who works under the supervision of the health care practitioner supervisor and performs only tasks delegated or directed by that supervisor (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). Certified Nurse Assistants (CNAs) and unlicensed assistive personnel are not assigned to perform in-home personal care services. Services that require a nurse are assigned only to a New Jersey-licensed nurse working within the scope of that license.

Corporate Compliance Policy 2 – Proof of New Jersey licensure or certification: Every licensed or certified staff member must show proof of current New Jersey licensure or certification before the first assignment and annually. Out-of-state certifications are not valid for New Jersey in-home personal care, and an out-of-state certificate does not qualify an aide for assignment. An aide who is in the process of applying for NJ certification may not be assigned until the NJ certificate is issued and verified.

definitions.definition: The type of service and the qualification of the worker needed, as set out in the client's plan of care, such as nursing services or aide personal care.
A nurse aide certified for facility settings, who is not, on that basis alone, authorized to provide in-home personal care for the agency.
Any worker without a nursing license or a current NJ CHHA certificate, such as a companion or sitter, who may not be assigned personal care.

definitions.term: Proof of NJ licensure or certification
definitions.definition: Primary-source verification of an active NJ license or CHHA certificate from the NJ Board of Nursing.
A certificate or license issued by another state, which is not valid on its own for NJ in-home personal care.

procedures: Human resources screens every applicant for a clinical or aide position and asks at the first contact for a copy of the NJ license or NJ Board of Nursing CHHA certificate. Applicants holding only a CNA, an out-of-state certificate or no certificate are told they cannot be assigned to in-home personal care.

Human resources verifies the NJ license or CHHA certificate with the NJ Board of Nursing (Call Center 973-504-6430, or its online verification) before an offer is made, and prints and dates the verification (see PER-03).
Human resources records the credential type, number and expiration date in the credential tracking log and in the personnel record. Only 'Active – NJ verified' staff can be scheduled.

At intake and assessment (CLN-01, CLN-03), the registered nurse identifies the level of care the client needs and writes it into the plan of care (CLN-04), specifying which tasks require a nurse and which may be delegated to a CHHA.

Before each new assignment, scheduling staff compare the credential on the tracking log to the level of care in the plan of care and record the match on the assignment form. If the credential does not match, the assignment is not made.

Scheduling staff do not use CNAs, home companions, sitters, trainees, students or any other unlicensed assistive personnel for personal care tasks (bathing, toileting, transferring, dressing, feeding, and similar tasks), even as a short-term substitute.

If no qualified worker is available, scheduling staff notify the Director of Nursing, who tells the client or representative and arranges rescheduling or another qualified agency employee. The notification is documented (CLN-12).
Nursing tasks are assigned only to a New Jersey-licensed nurse. The Director of Nursing confirms that the nurse's license is active and the task is within scope.

Human resources re-verifies each licensed or certified employee's NJ credential at least once every 12 months and before the credential's expiration date (PER-03, PER-11). A person whose credential lapses is removed from the schedule that day.
Employees must report immediately any change in their license or certificate status, including expiration, renewal, discipline or an out-of-state move. Failure to report is grounds for discipline.

The Director of Nursing spot-checks at least 10 percent of active assignments each quarter, comparing the assigned worker's credential with the plan of care's level of care, and reports the results to the quality assurance committee (ADM-14).

If a mismatch is found, the Director of Nursing removes the worker from the assignment at once, arranges a qualified replacement, assesses the client for any harm, files an incident report (SAF-02) and notifies the Administrator, who decides on reporting under ADM-06.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy is applied and takes corrective action on mismatches or unverified credentials.

responsibilities.role: Director of Nursing/Health Care Practitioner Supervisor
responsibilities.duty: Defines the level of care in the plan of care, approves assignments and performs quarterly spot checks.
Verifies NJ licensure and certification before hire and annually, and keeps the credential tracking log.
Match credential to level of care before every assignment and never assign CNAs or unlicensed staff to personal care.
Keep credentials active and report changes at once.

documentation: NJ Board of Nursing verification (dated) for each licensed or certified employee
Credential tracking log
Assignment forms showing level-of-care match
Plans of care specifying level of care and delegated tasks
Annual re-verification records
Quarterly assignment audit reports
Incident reports and corrective action records for any mismatch

policies.title: Client Complaints and Grievances
policies.applies_to: Administrator, compliance officer, Director of Nursing/Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, Nurse Supervisors, intake and scheduling staff, and all employees who may receive a complaint
policies.purpose: To make sure clients, families, representatives and staff can report complaints to [AGENCY NAME] without fear of retaliation, that every complaint is logged, investigated and resolved, and that Medicaid MCO members know how to use the MCO grievance process.
policies.policy:
This policy meets Best Practices §IV, Corporate Compliance Policy 3 – Reporting of patient complaints to the agency.

Clients, family members, authorized representatives and staff may make a complaint to [AGENCY NAME] at any time, orally or in writing, about services, staff conduct, scheduling, billing, privacy or any other concern. The agency logs every complaint, investigates it, takes corrective action when appropriate, and documents the outcome. No one is penalized or has services reduced for making a complaint (see CR-01 and ADM-07).

Nurse Supervisors ask about complaints at the 30-day contact and at the 60-day in-home evaluation of the plan of care (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(c), (d) and (g)), and record the client's responses and any complaint in the client record. Clients who receive services through NJ FamilyCare managed care (including MLTSS) are told how to use the MCO's grievance and appeal process and that using the agency's process does not replace or delay their right to use it. This policy supports the rights of Medicaid home and community-based services participants under 42 CFR 441.301(c).

If a complaint alleges abuse, neglect or exploitation, it is handled immediately under SAF-01 and SAF-02.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency or its staff, whether or not the person calls it a complaint and whether made orally or in writing.
A complaint that is formally logged and investigated through the process in this policy, or the formal process through a managed care organization.
The client, family member, authorized representative, employee or other person who raises the complaint.
A health plan contracted with NJ FamilyCare to cover services for enrolled members, including MLTSS.
The registered nurse or health care practitioner supervisor responsible for supervising the plan of care and the aide.

procedures: At admission, intake staff gives each client or representative the written complaint procedure, including the agency's complaint line [PHONE], email [EMAIL], address [ADDRESS], and the name of the person who handles complaints ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]). Staff explain it orally and record that it was given (CR-01).

For clients who are NJ FamilyCare MCO members, intake staff also give the MCO's grievance and appeal contact information, explain that the client may go to the MCO at any time, and record the explanation. Information is provided in the client's language and in an accessible format (CR-02).

Any employee who receives a complaint accepts it respectfully, records the key facts and logs it the same day on the complaint log with date, complainant, client, summary and who received it. Employees do not argue with or discourage the complainant.

Employees tell the Director of Nursing right away of any complaint that involves client safety, quality of care, abuse, neglect or exploitation. In those cases, the Director of Nursing takes protective steps at once and starts SAF-01 and SAF-02.
The complaint handler (the Administrator or designee) acknowledges the complaint to the complainant within 2 business days, by telephone or in writing, and says who will investigate.

The complaint handler investigates by reviewing records, interviewing the client, the aide and others, and reviewing visit and timekeeping data as appropriate. A person named in a complaint does not investigate it.

The complaint handler tries to resolve the complaint and tells the complainant of the outcome, in writing when asked, within 14 days of receipt. If more time is needed, the complainant is told why and given a new date. The agency's time frame is an internal standard and does not limit the time under any MCO grievance process.

If resolution requires a change in the aide, the schedule or the plan of care, the Director of Nursing arranges it and, if the plan of care must be revised, a licensed person reassesses it immediately (CLN-04, CLN-08).

Nurse Supervisors ask the client or representative at each 30-day contact whether they have any concerns about services or staff, and record the response, including any complaint, in the client record (CLN-08).

Nurse Supervisors repeat the question during the 60-day in-home evaluation of the plan of care and document any complaint and the action taken (CLN-08). Complaints found at either contact are entered in the complaint log the same day.

If the complainant is not satisfied, the complaint handler refers it to the Administrator and, if needed, the governing body for review. The complainant is told they may also contact the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs at (973) 504-6370 or, for concerns about a CHHA's certification, the NJ Board of Nursing at 973-504-6430, or, for MCO members, the MCO grievance process.
The complaint handler documents the investigation, findings, resolution and communication with the complainant in the complaint file, and the log is closed only after the outcome has been recorded.

If a complaint involves a Medicaid-covered service and is about services not authorized, denied or reduced, the complaint handler refers the client to the MCO or care manager for the authorization and appeal process (MED-03). The agency does not discourage the client from appealing.

The compliance officer reviews the complaint log monthly for trends, such as repeat complaints about one aide, late visits or billing, and gives the quality assurance committee a quarterly summary (ADM-14). Trends lead to documented corrective action and staff retraining.
Complaint records are kept in a file apart from the clinical record, with a note in the client record that a complaint was received, and are retained under REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees the complaint process, reviews unresolved complaints and ensures corrective action.
Maintains the complaint log, reviews trends monthly and reports to quality assurance.

responsibilities.role: Director of Nursing/Health Care Practitioner Supervisor
responsibilities.duty: Responds to clinical and safety complaints, arranges changes in staffing or the plan of care.
Ask about complaints at the 30-day contact and 60-day in-home evaluation, and document responses.
Give the complaint procedure and MCO grievance information at admission.
Accept and report every complaint the same day and never retaliate.

documentation: Complaint procedure acknowledgment in the client record
MCO grievance information provided (for MCO members)
Complaint log
Investigation notes, findings and resolution letters or call notes
30-day contact and 60-day re-evaluation notes recording client responses and complaints
Corrective action and retraining records
Quarterly complaint trend summary for quality assurance

policies.title: Confidentiality, Privacy and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] owners, governing body members, administrators, nurses, Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs), office staff, contractors and volunteers; all client and employee information in any form (paper, electronic, verbal)
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of client and employee information, to disclose it only as permitted, and to comply with the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules.
policies.policy: This policy meets Best Practices §IV, Corporate Compliance Policy 5 — Confidentiality requirements. [AGENCY NAME] safeguards all client and employee information and discloses it only as permitted by HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), New Jersey law and the client's written authorization. Staff access only the minimum information needed to do their jobs. A copy of each client's plan of care is kept at the residence and is available to the client, the family or representative and the employees who serve that client. The agency must still protect that copy from view by anyone who is not entitled to see it. The record of each task delegated to a CHHA is kept in the client's record under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7 and is protected in the same way. HIPAA and confidentiality are mandatory orientation topics (see PER-06). Violations are investigated and sanctioned, up to and including termination.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health, care, payment or demographic information about a client, in any form.
The least amount of PHI needed to accomplish a permitted purpose.
An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of unsecured PHI that compromises its privacy or security, unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability of compromise.
The person designated by the Administrator to oversee privacy compliance, complaints and breach response.
A vendor or contractor that creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI for the agency (for example billing, software, EVV or payroll vendors).

procedures: The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer and a Security Officer in writing ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]) and posts their contact information for staff and clients.
Before services begin, office staff give each client or representative the agency's Notice of Privacy Practices, obtain a signed acknowledgment, and file it in the client record.

Office staff obtain a written, signed HIPAA authorization before disclosing PHI for any purpose other than treatment, payment, health care operations or disclosures required by law. The authorization states who receives the information, what is shared, the purpose, the expiration and the right to revoke. The Privacy Officer reviews every non-routine request.

Staff disclose PHI without authorization only when permitted. Permitted disclosures include coordination with the client's physician, practitioner supervisor or care manager; billing to NJ FamilyCare, MCOs or the Personal Preference Program fiscal intermediary; reports of abuse, neglect or exploitation (SAF-01); and disclosures to the Division of Consumer Affairs, the Board of Nursing or other regulators. Each disclosure is limited to the minimum necessary.

Orientation (PER-06) includes HIPAA and confidentiality training. Each employee signs a confidentiality agreement and the signed form is placed in the personnel record. Training is repeated annually in-service (PER-07) and whenever the policy changes.

CHHAs discuss client information only with the supervising nurse, the on-call RN or the client's authorized representatives. They do not discuss clients in public places, with other clients or on social media, and they do not photograph or record clients or their homes.
The plan of care copy kept in the home is left in a place agreed on with the client. It is not left in view of visitors, and the CHHA does not remove it from the home.
Paper records are stored in locked cabinets in a locked office. Staff do not leave records in vehicles or unattended in homes.

Electronic PHI is protected by unique user IDs, role-based access, strong passwords, automatic log-off, encryption of laptops and phones, and regular backups. The Security Officer removes access on the day of an employee's separation or role change.
Staff use only agency-approved secure messaging, telephone or email for PHI. Client names and details are not sent by unsecured text or personal email.
The Administrator signs a business associate agreement with every vendor that handles PHI before it is given access, and keeps the agreements on file.

Clients or representatives may ask to inspect or obtain a copy of their record, request amendments or request an accounting of disclosures. The Privacy Officer responds in writing within the time HIPAA allows, and documents the request and response.

Employee records (applications, health attestations, TB results, background checks, wage records) are kept in separate, locked personnel files with access limited to the Administrator, the DON/HCSS and designated HR staff.

Any staff member who suspects a privacy or security incident reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the work day. The Privacy Officer opens an investigation, mitigates harm, and completes and documents a four-factor breach risk assessment.

If a breach of unsecured PHI is confirmed, the Privacy Officer notifies affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery. The Privacy Officer also notifies the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and any other party required by HIPAA, a contract or New Jersey law. The agency keeps a log of all breaches.

The Administrator applies written sanctions consistently to any workforce member who violates this policy: retraining, written warning, suspension or termination, depending on severity and intent. Sanctions are recorded in the personnel record. No one is retaliated against for reporting a privacy concern (see ADM-07).
The Privacy Officer conducts and documents a privacy and security audit at least annually and reports results to the governing body through the QA program (ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Privacy and Security Officers, enforces sanctions, signs business associate agreements and reports privacy results to the governing body.
Manages authorizations, record access requests, complaints, breach investigations and notifications, and annual audits.
Maintains electronic safeguards, access controls and backups.
Ensures nursing staff and CHHAs follow confidentiality rules in the field, including handling of the in-home plan of care copy.
Protect PHI, access only what they need, and report suspected incidents immediately.

documentation: Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments
Signed HIPAA authorizations
Employee confidentiality agreements and HIPAA training records
Business associate agreements
Record access, amendment and accounting-of-disclosure logs
Privacy incident and breach risk assessments and breach log
Sanction records
Annual privacy and security audit reports

policies.title: Clinical On-Call Coverage
policies.applies_to: All RNs, LPNs, CHHAs and other clinical staff; the DON/HCSS and Administrator; all clients receiving services
policies.purpose: To ensure that clinical staff can always reach a registered nurse for clinical questions while services are being provided.
policies.policy: This policy meets Best Practices §IV, Clinical On-Call Policy: a procedure by which an RN, LPN, CHHA or other clinical staff can reach an RN for clinical questions at all times, in no less than one hour, with an RN on call during all hours of service. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a registered nurse on call during every hour that any client is receiving services, including nights, weekends and holidays. Any clinical staff member can reach the on-call RN, and the RN responds immediately for urgent matters and in every case within one hour. The on-call number is published to all staff and clients, and every call is logged. The on-call RN may direct a CHHA only within the tasks that have been delegated and recorded by the practitioner supervisor (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). Emergencies are never held for a call-back: staff call 911 first (see CLN-13).

definitions.definition: A New Jersey-licensed registered nurse designated on the published schedule to answer clinical questions and direct staff during the coverage period.
Any time at which a CHHA or other clinical staff member is scheduled to be, or is, providing care to a client.
Any question about a client's condition, the plan of care, delegated tasks, medication assistance, equipment, infection control or safety.

procedures: The DON/HCSS prepares a written on-call schedule at least two weeks ahead, assigning a New Jersey-licensed RN and a named backup RN to every hour that services are scheduled. The schedule contains no gaps.

The agency maintains a dedicated on-call telephone number ([ON-CALL PHONE]), forwarded to the on-call RN's phone at the start of each shift. The RN must have the capability to access the client's record, plan of care and delegation list remotely.

The on-call number is printed on every employee ID badge card or wallet card, on the staff handbook and on the client's service agreement and plan of care copy kept in the home. It is given verbally at orientation (PER-06) and is repeated at each in-service.

Staff call the on-call RN for any clinical question, a change in a client's condition (CLN-13), questions about whether a task is within the plan of care or delegation, medication assistance questions, and any other clinical concern.

The on-call RN answers calls immediately for urgent matters. If the RN cannot answer, the call goes to voicemail and the RN calls back as soon as possible, in all cases no later than one hour after the call was placed.
If the RN has not called back within 30 minutes, the caller phones the backup RN, and then the DON/HCSS. The Administrator is contacted if neither is reached within one hour.
For a life-threatening emergency, staff call 911 first and then notify the on-call RN. Staff never wait for a call-back before calling 911.

The on-call RN gives direction only within the CHHA's scope: the tasks delegated and documented by the practitioner supervisor, and the plan of care. The RN does not authorize tasks outside the delegation. When a new task is needed, the RN arranges the supervisory assessment, delegation and competency demonstration (CLN-05, CLN-06) before the CHHA performs it.

The on-call RN records every call in the on-call log, noting date, time received, time returned, caller, client, question, advice or direction given, and any follow-up. The RN completes the entry before the shift ends.

Any call that results in a change to the client's care, an incident or a physician contact is also documented in the client's record by the RN, and the DON/HCSS is notified the next business day (SAF-02 if an incident).
The on-call RN hands off open issues to the next on-call RN at the shift change, in writing or by recorded verbal report.
The DON/HCSS reviews the on-call log weekly and checks response times. Any response longer than one hour is investigated and addressed with the RN involved.
The DON/HCSS tests the on-call system at least quarterly by placing an unannounced test call, and documents the result.
If the on-call RN becomes unavailable (illness, a dropped phone, an emergency), the RN or DON/HCSS immediately activates the backup RN and updates the call forwarding.
On-call response times, call volume and trends are reported to the QA committee quarterly (ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Builds the schedule, assigns backups, audits the log and tests the system.
Remains reachable, responds within one hour, directs staff within delegated tasks, logs every call and documents in the client record when needed.
Covers when the primary RN does not respond in 30 minutes or is unavailable.
Call the on-call RN for clinical questions, follow the direction given and call 911 in emergencies.
Ensures that RN staffing is sufficient to cover every hour of service and that the number is published.

documentation: Written on-call schedule with backup RN
On-call log (date, time received, time returned, caller, client, question, direction, follow-up)
Quarterly test call records
Entries in the client record for calls that change care
Weekly log review notes and QA reports

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: All clients and families; the Administrator, intake and billing staff; private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and Personal Preference Program clients
policies.purpose: To make sure that patients, families and significant others receive full and truthful disclosure of all fees and billing policies before services begin, and that the agency never charges improper fees or bills for unauthorized services.
policies.policy: This policy meets Best Practices §IV, Service Agreement Policy: patients and family/significant others are provided with full and truthful disclosure of all information concerning fees and billing policies. Before services begin, [AGENCY NAME] gives every client or representative a written service agreement stating the rate, minimum visit length, cancellation terms, services included and excluded, billing terms and the complaint process. The agency gives complete and accurate information and does not use misleading statements in conversations, advertising or invoices. The Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides is included in the packet and is provided at least 24 hours before services unless the 24-hour timing is waived in writing (see ADM-13, N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7). The agency charges no placement fee, liquidated damages or other fee to an employee in connection with employment, and does not prevent an employee by contract from working for others, because the agency does not hold an employment agency license (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6). For Medicaid PCA, MLTSS and PPP clients, the agency bills only for authorized services actually delivered within the authorized hours, and gives plan members information consistent with the managed care enrollee information requirements (42 CFR 438.10).

definitions.definition: The written contract between the agency and the client or representative stating the services, rates, billing and rights of each party.
Services paid for by the client or family rather than by Medicaid, an MCO or another third party.
The hours and tasks approved by NJ FamilyCare, the MCO or the PPP program in the client's authorization or care plan.
The shortest scheduled visit that the agency will staff, stated in the agreement.

procedures: The Administrator approves a written rate schedule ([RATE SCHEDULE]) and a standard service agreement template, reviews them at least annually and when rates change, and keeps dated versions.

At the intake interview (CLN-01), intake staff explain the rates, minimum visit length, cancellation terms, billing terms, services included and excluded, and the complaint process orally and in plain language. An interpreter or translated copy is used when needed (CR-02).

For private-pay clients, the service agreement lists the hourly rate, any different rate for nights, weekends or holidays, the minimum hours per visit, the cancellation notice period and any cancellation charge ([CANCELLATION TERMS]), the billing cycle, payment methods, late fees if any, and how rate changes are announced (written notice of [NUMBER] days).

The agreement lists services included (consistent with the plan of care and with CLN-10) and services excluded (for example, skilled nursing tasks not delegated, transporting clients if not offered, and any task outside the CHHA scope). Where the agency does not provide a service, the agreement says so.

For Medicaid PCA, MLTSS and PPP clients, the agreement or intake packet states that the client pays no fee for covered authorized services, identifies the payer, and explains that services are limited to the authorized hours and tasks (MED-01, MED-03). Staff do not ask Medicaid clients for supplemental payments for covered services.

The packet includes the Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides, the client rights statement (CR-01), the Notice of Privacy Practices (ADM-10), the complaint procedure (ADM-09) and the on-call number (ADM-11).

The agency delivers the packet, including the Consumer Guide, at least 24 hours before services start. If the client waives the timing in writing, the agency still delivers the packet before services begin (ADM-13).

The client or representative signs and dates the agreement before the first visit. The agency gives a copy to the client and places the original in the client record. No visit is staffed until the agreement is signed, except where the client's urgent safety need requires it and the RN documents the reason and obtains the signature at the first visit.

The Administrator does not charge any employee a placement fee, registration fee, training fee, liquidated damages or other fee connected with employment, and does not include any clause preventing an employee from working for other employers or clients. Employment forms are reviewed by the Administrator before use (PER-01, PER-12).

Billing staff invoice only for services documented as delivered, matched to the CHHA's weekly activity record (CLN-07) and EVV or timekeeping data (CLN-12). Invoices show the dates, hours, rates and total.

For Medicaid clients, billing staff compare each claim against the current authorization before submission. Hours beyond the authorization, tasks outside the plan of care, and visits that cannot be verified are never billed. If a client needs more hours, staff contact the care manager or MCO to request a revision (MED-03).
Before changing a rate or policy, the Administrator gives the client written notice of at least [NUMBER] days. A client who does not accept the change may end services under CLN-14.

Staff who receive a billing question or dispute refer it to the billing manager. The billing manager responds in writing within [NUMBER] business days, corrects any error, and issues refunds or credits promptly. Unresolved disputes are handled under the complaint procedure (ADM-09).

Any overpayment, whether from a client or a payer, is identified, documented and returned promptly. The Administrator reports Medicaid overpayments according to the corporate compliance program (ADM-06).
The billing manager audits a sample of invoices and Medicaid claims against records each quarter. Findings go to the QA committee (ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Approves rates and agreement templates, ensures no prohibited employee fees, and resolves billing disputes.
Explain fees and policies accurately, deliver the packet and obtain signatures.
Invoices only authorized, documented services and handles billing questions and corrections.
Ensures the services listed in the agreement match the plan of care and scope.

documentation: Signed service agreement with the client record
Rate schedule with revision dates
Packet receipt, including the Consumer Guide delivery date and any written 24-hour waiver (ADM-13)
Invoices and payment records
Medicaid authorization compared with claims
Billing dispute and refund records
Quarterly billing audit reports

policies.title: Caregiver ID Tags and Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides
policies.applies_to: All CHHAs and regulated health care professionals (RNs, LPNs) employed by [AGENCY NAME] who provide care; intake staff; the Administrator and DON/HCSS; all patient/employers
policies.purpose: To ensure that every caregiver is clearly identified at all times in the home and that every patient/employer receives the Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide at least 24 hours before services, as required by N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(a), (b), (c) and (d). (a) Every certified homemaker-home health aide and every regulated health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME] wears an identification tag at all times while providing care. The tag shows the person's first name or initial, full surname, the term for the level of licensure or certification (for example 'Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide' or 'Registered Nurse'), and a photograph. All letters are the same size and no smaller than one-quarter inch, and the tag is at least as large as any other identification worn. (b) The agency provides every patient/employer with a copy of the Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides published by the New Jersey Board of Nursing. (c) The Consumer Guide is provided at least 24 hours before services are provided. (d) A patient/employer may waive the 24-hour timing in writing. The agency keeps the waiver for at least two years and still provides the Consumer Guide before services begin.

definitions.definition: The client, or the client's representative, who receives services from, or directly engages, the aide.
The Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides published by the New Jersey Board of Nursing.
The term identifying the person's credential, such as Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide, Licensed Practical Nurse or Registered Nurse.
A written statement signed and dated by the patient/employer agreeing to receive the Consumer Guide fewer than 24 hours before services begin.

procedures: ID tag (item 13:45B-13.7(a)): Before an employee's first client assignment, the DON/HCSS or designated office staff verifies the person's active certification or license (PER-03) and takes a clear, current, front-facing photograph.

Office staff prepare the tag with the employee's first name or initial and full surname, the correct credential term (for example 'Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide'), and the photograph. All lettering is equal in size and at least one-quarter inch high. Staff measure the letters on the first printed tag and keep the template.

The agency's tag template is designed so that the tag is at least as large as any other ID worn. Employees do not wear a facility badge, client-issued ID or other ID that is larger than the agency tag while on assignment. If a facility requires its own badge, the office issues an agency tag at least as large as that badge.

Employees wear the tag visibly on the upper body at all times while providing care, including the entire visit. Employees do not cover, alter or lend their tag. The supervisor's field observation (CLN-09) includes a check of the tag.

A lost, damaged or illegible tag is reported to the office the same day. The office issues a replacement before the next visit. When a credential level or name changes, or the certification lapses or is not renewed, the office collects and replaces or voids the tag (PER-11).
Office staff keep a tag issuance log with date, employee, credential term, and replacement or return dates. Tags are collected at separation.

Consumer Guide (items 13:45B-13.7(b) and (c)): The Administrator obtains the current edition of the Consumer Guide from the Board of Nursing (Division of Consumer Affairs website, Board of Nursing call center 973-504-6430) and checks quarterly that the agency is using the current edition. Superseded editions are removed from use.

Intake staff give each patient/employer a copy of the Consumer Guide, in print or by another method the client can use, with the service agreement packet (ADM-12). Delivery must take place at least 24 hours before the first service. Intake staff schedule the first visit no earlier than 24 hours after the delivery time unless a written waiver is obtained.

Intake staff record in the client record the date and time the Guide was delivered, the method (hand delivery, mail, email with confirmation) and the staff member. For clients who do not read English or have a disability, staff provide the Guide in an accessible format or review it with the aid of an interpreter (CR-02).

Waiver (item 13:45B-13.7(d)): If the patient/employer wants services to begin sooner than 24 hours after receiving the Guide, intake staff ask them to sign and date a written waiver stating that they waive only the 24-hour timing. The client does not waive receipt of the Guide, and staff never suggest that the Guide is optional.

The agency delivers the Consumer Guide to the client before the first service begins, even if a waiver is signed. The first visit does not start until delivery is documented. The CHHA confirms at the first visit that the client has the Guide, and calls the office if not.

The waiver is filed in the client record and kept for at least two years from the date signed (the agency's general retention rule in REC-01 may require longer). The office keeps a waiver log for audit.

For each new admission, the DON/HCSS or designee audits that the tag requirements were met and that the Consumer Guide was delivered at least 24 hours before services or a signed waiver is on file with documented delivery before services began.

Any audit failure is corrected immediately: the tag is replaced, the Guide is delivered and the client is told. The Administrator documents the corrective action and reports trends to the QA committee (ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the agency has the current Consumer Guide, enforces this policy and signs off on QA findings.
Verifies credentials before tags are issued, observes tag use in the field and audits admissions.
Deliver the Guide at least 24 hours before services, obtain and file waivers, and document delivery.
Prepare compliant tags, keep the issuance log and collect tags at separation.
Wear the tag at all times while giving care, report loss or damage the same day, and confirm the client has the Guide.

documentation: ID tag issuance log and tag template
Employee photograph and credential verification (PER-03)
Consumer Guide delivery record (date, time, method, staff)
Signed written waivers, kept at least two years
Admission audit checklists
Corrective action records

policies.title: Quality Assurance, Performance Improvement and Policy Review
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] governing body, Administrator, DON/HCSS, QA committee and all staff
policies.purpose: To monitor the quality, safety and regulatory compliance of services, correct problems promptly and keep this Policy & Procedure Manual current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates a quality assurance and performance improvement (QAPI) program overseen by the governing body. The program audits client and personnel files and field practice on a regular schedule. It checks that the plan of care is written by an appropriately licensed person before placement, signed with license designation, matched by the level of care placed, reviewed by a 30-day inquiry and a 60-day in-home evaluation, and that copies are given to the patient or representative (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9). The program also audits delegation and supervision files: every task listed, documented and signed. It verifies that only actively certified CHHAs are scheduled and that PCA clients have a current certification of need. It tracks accreditation and the documents required for registration renewal, including evidence of accreditation and financial statements (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5). The manual is reviewed at least annually and whenever a rule changes, with version control.

definitions.definition: The group, chaired by the Administrator or DON/HCSS, that reviews audit results and directs corrective action.
A written plan stating the problem, root cause, actions, responsible person and due date.
A system that gives each policy a version number, effective date and approval record, and retains superseded versions.
The physician or practitioner certification required for Medicaid PCA services (see MED-01).

procedures: The governing body approves the written QAPI plan annually. The plan names the QA committee members (Administrator, DON/HCSS, a billing or HR representative and, when possible, a client representative) and sets the audit calendar.
The QA committee meets at least quarterly. Minutes record the data reviewed, findings, decisions and assigned actions, and are kept on file.

Plan of care audit (monthly): The DON/HCSS reviews a sample of at least 10% of active records, no fewer than five. For each record, the reviewer checks that an appropriately licensed person evaluated the patient's needs and wrote the plan before placement, that the preparer signed with license designation, and that the level of care placed matches the plan.

Periodic review audit (monthly): For each sampled record, the reviewer confirms that the supervisor made an inquiry at least once in every 30-day period about whether the plan is adequate and being carried out, and recorded the answers. The reviewer also confirms an on-site in-home evaluation at least once in every 60-day period (CLN-08).

Plan revision and correction audit: The reviewer checks that any plan needing revision was reassessed immediately by a licensed person, that corrective action was immediate when a plan was not carried out properly, and that the original and each revised plan are in the record and copies were given to the patient or representative.

Delegation and supervision file audit (monthly): For every CHHA assigned to sampled clients, the reviewer confirms that each task the CHHA performs is listed on the delegation record, documented in the client's record, signed by the supervisor and supported by a demonstrated competency (CLN-05, CLN-06, PER-09). Any task performed but not listed is a finding.

Certification verification (monthly): The reviewer compares the schedule for the last 30 days against the Board of Nursing certification status for each CHHA scheduled. No visit may have been staffed by a CHHA without active certification (PER-03, PER-11, ADM-08).

Medicaid PCA audit (monthly): For PCA clients, the reviewer verifies a current certification of need, a current authorization, RN assessment and supervision, and that billed hours do not exceed authorized hours (MED-01, MED-02, ADM-12).

Operational indicators (quarterly): The committee reviews missed visits, late visits, complaints and grievances, incidents, abuse/neglect reports, on-call response times, change-in-condition events, infection events, staff turnover and client satisfaction results.

Registration and accreditation readiness (quarterly): The Administrator reports to the committee on the registration expiration date, accreditation status and survey dates, and readiness of the financial statements and other documents that must be submitted at renewal, including evidence of accreditation (ADM-02, ADM-05).

For every finding, the committee assigns a CAP with an owner and due date, usually within 30 days. Any finding that affects client safety (an unlisted task, uncertified aide, missed 60-day evaluation) is corrected immediately and the client is protected first.
The DON/HCSS follows up on each CAP and re-audits within 60 days. Items not resolved are escalated to the Administrator and the governing body.

Annual policy review: The Administrator assigns each policy to an owner and the committee reviews the entire manual at least once every 12 months. The review also takes place whenever a statute, regulation, payer rule or agency practice changes, within [30] days of becoming aware of the change.

Version control: Each policy shows a policy number, version, effective date, reviewer and approver. Revised policies are approved by the Administrator and governing body, superseded versions are archived, and the revision log is kept.

Staff are trained on a revised policy before its effective date or at the next scheduled in-service, and acknowledge it in writing (PER-07). The Administrator replaces outdated copies in the office and in staff access locations.
The Administrator provides the governing body with an annual QAPI report, including trends, corrective actions, and policy changes. The report is retained for at least [NUMBER] years.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the QAPI plan, receives reports and ensures resources for corrective action.
Leads the QA committee, owns policy version control and registration/accreditation readiness.
Conducts clinical file audits, certifications checks and follow-up on CAPs.
Reviews data, assigns corrective actions and verifies resolution.
Cooperate with audits, report concerns and complete training on revised policies.

documentation: QAPI plan and audit calendar
Audit tools and completed audit worksheets
QA committee minutes
Corrective action plans and re-audit results
Annual QAPI report
Policy master list with version, effective date and approvals
Policy revision log and staff acknowledgments of revised policies

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All clients and their representatives; all [AGENCY NAME] staff
policies.purpose: To inform each client of their rights and responsibilities before services start and to protect those rights throughout the service relationship.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives every client or representative a written statement of rights and responsibilities before services start, together with the Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7). Clients and families receive copies of the plan of care; the agency keeps the original and any revised plan and gives copies to the patient or representative (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9). Clients may refuse any service and may complain or ask questions without fear of retaliation. For clients receiving Medicaid home and community-based services, the agency supports the client's choices, privacy, dignity and person-centered planning in line with 42 CFR 441.301(c), and honors the privacy rights stated in HIPAA (45 CFR Part 164).

definitions.definition: The written list of rights and responsibilities given to the client or representative, signed for receipt.
A person legally authorized to act for the client, such as a guardian or agent under a power of attorney or health care proxy.
Any adverse action, such as reduced service, threats, harsher treatment or discharge, taken because a client or family member complained or exercised a right.
The written plan prepared and signed by an appropriately licensed person before placement (see CLN-04).

procedures: At the intake interview (CLN-01), intake staff review the client rights and responsibilities statement with the client or representative, in plain language and in the client's preferred language, with an interpreter or translated copy when needed (CR-02).

The client or representative signs and dates an acknowledgment of receipt. The original goes in the client record and a copy remains with the client. If the client cannot sign, staff record the reason and the name of the person who received the statement.

The agency gives the Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides at least 24 hours before services begin, together with the rights statement, unless the client signs a written waiver of the timing. The Guide is still given before services begin (ADM-13).

The rights statement includes the right to: be treated with dignity and respect and free from abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination; have privacy and confidentiality of information and property; take part in planning care; know the name, title and credential of each caregiver, shown on the ID tag; receive services within the plan of care; know all fees before services begin (ADM-12); and refuse any service or ask that a caregiver be changed.

It also states the right to receive a copy of the plan of care and any revisions; to be told promptly of changes in services or in the caregiver; to access and ask for correction of one's records under HIPAA (ADM-10); to be told how to contact the on-call RN (ADM-11); and to receive advance notice of a discharge or transfer (CLN-14).

The statement also describes the client's responsibilities: give accurate information about health and medication; tell the agency of changes in condition, hospitalizations or insurance; provide a safe home environment; treat staff with respect; keep agreed schedules or give notice of cancellations; and meet the payment terms in the service agreement.

After the plan of care is written and signed by the licensed preparer, the agency gives copies to the client or representative. The agency also places a copy at the residence, available to the client, the family and employees. When the plan is revised, the agency issues the revised plan and gives copies promptly (CLN-04).

A client may refuse any service, medication assistance or treatment without penalty. When a client refuses, the caregiver respects the decision, ensures the client is safe, notes the refusal and calls the supervising nurse or the on-call RN, who explains the risks, informs the practitioner or care manager as required, and updates the plan if the client's wishes have changed (CLN-13).

Clients may complain to any staff member, the DON/HCSS or the Administrator at any time, orally or in writing. Staff forward every complaint on the same day to the Administrator, who handles it under ADM-09.

The rights statement and the complaint procedure give the contact information for the agency ([PHONE]). They also list outside agencies: the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs, Regulated Business Section ((973) 504-6370), which registers health care service firms; the NJ Board of Nursing (973-504-6430), for concerns about a CHHA's certification or conduct; and, for Medicaid clients, the client's NJ FamilyCare managed care organization or care manager.

Staff must not retaliate against a client or family member who files a complaint, refuses a service or contacts a regulator. Retaliation is a conduct violation and results in disciplinary action up to termination (PER-13). Suspected retaliation is reported to the Administrator immediately.
Staff report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of any client immediately under SAF-01, whether or not the client has complained.

The DON/HCSS reviews the client record at the 60-day in-home evaluation (CLN-08) to confirm the client still has the rights statement, the Consumer Guide and the current plan of care, and asks the client if their rights are being respected.

The Administrator reviews complaints, refusals and rights concerns quarterly and reports trends to the QA committee (ADM-14). Rights training is part of orientation (PER-06) and annual in-service (PER-07).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the rights statement is current, handles complaints and prohibits retaliation.
Review and deliver the rights statement and Consumer Guide, and obtain signed acknowledgments.
Ensures plan of care copies are given and kept in the home, and responds to refusals and rights concerns.
Respect client rights, honor refusals, safeguard privacy and report complaints and suspected abuse the same day.
Follow the stated responsibilities and share information needed for safe care.

documentation: Signed rights and responsibilities acknowledgment
Consumer Guide delivery record and any written waiver (ADM-13)
Plan of care copy-distribution record
Client refusal notes and nursing follow-up
Complaint log and resolution records (ADM-09)
Records of rights training for staff

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs), nurse supervisors, intake and scheduling staff, and all applicants for and recipients of services (private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and Personal Preference Program participants)
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who seeks or receives services from [AGENCY NAME] is treated without discrimination, can communicate with the agency in a language and format they understand at no cost, and receives reasonable accommodations for disability.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin (including limited English proficiency), sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability, religion, marital status, source of payment or any other characteristic protected by federal or New Jersey law. This applies to inquiry, intake, eligibility for services, caregiver assignment, service delivery, transfer and discharge. This policy implements Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act. [AGENCY NAME] provides qualified interpreter services, translated vital documents, and accessible materials and auxiliary aids at no cost to the client. It documents every reasonable accommodation requested and provided. Client preferences about a caregiver (for example, same-gender personal care or language) may be honored when they relate to dignity, comfort or communication. Preferences based on a protected characteristic such as race or religion will not be used to assign or refuse staff.

definitions.definition: A person whose primary language is not English and who has a limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.

A person who is fluent in English and the client's language, is trained in interpreting skills and medical terminology, and follows confidentiality and impartiality standards. Bilingual ability alone does not qualify a staff member.

A document that is critical to accessing services or that must be understood to give consent, such as the service agreement, client rights notice, plan of care summary, consent and authorization forms, grievance procedure and discharge notice.

A device or service that makes communication effective for people with disabilities, such as large print, braille, sign language interpreters, captioning, screen-reader-compatible files or relay services.

A change to a policy, practice or procedure, or the provision of an aid, that lets a person with a disability access and benefit from services, unless it would fundamentally alter the service or cause an undue burden.

procedures: The Administrator designates a nondiscrimination and language access coordinator, [SECTION 1557 COORDINATOR NAME], [PHONE], who receives complaints, tracks accommodation requests and keeps this policy current. The designation is recorded in the administrative file.

At first contact, intake staff ask every inquirer for their preferred language for spoken and written communication and whether they need any accommodation or accessible format. The answers are recorded on the intake record (see CLN-02).

If the client or representative is LEP or deaf or hard of hearing, intake staff arrange a qualified interpreter (telephone, video or in-person) or auxiliary aid before the intake interview and nursing assessment. The agency pays the cost. No charge is passed to the client or the payer.

Staff do not require or encourage a client to bring a family member or friend to interpret. A family member or friend may interpret only if the client requests it after being told a free qualified interpreter is available. The request is documented. Minor children are not used as interpreters except in a genuine emergency until a qualified interpreter is available.

Bilingual employees interpret only after the Administrator or DON confirms and documents their language proficiency and interpreter training. Their interpreting must not interfere with their assigned duties.

Vital documents (see Definitions) are provided in the client's language. Where a written translation is not available for a language, staff use a qualified interpreter to give the client an oral translation of the document. This is documented.

The agency's notice of nondiscrimination and language assistance (including how to obtain services and file a grievance) is included in the admission packet, posted in the office, and posted on the agency website in the languages most commonly spoken in the agency's service area.

When a client or applicant requests an accommodation or accessible format, the nurse supervisor or coordinator evaluates the request within 2 business days. Staff provide the accommodation unless it would be an undue burden or a fundamental alteration. If a request is denied, the Administrator documents the reasons and offers an effective alternative.

Each accommodation requested, the decision, the date implemented and who provided it are documented in the client record and on the accommodation log. Accommodations that affect care (for example, communication methods) are added to the plan of care (see CLN-04).

Intake and scheduling decisions are based on the clinical needs of the client, the services authorized, staff availability and competency, and the geographic service area. A client is never refused, delayed or assigned lower-quality service because of a protected characteristic, payer or language. If the agency cannot serve a client for a nondiscriminatory reason such as capacity or service area, staff refer the client to other resources and document the referral.

Transfer, discontinuation and discharge decisions follow CLN-14. The nurse supervisor and Administrator review each involuntary discharge before notice is given to confirm the reason is not discriminatory.

A staff member who is asked to treat a client differently because of a protected characteristic (for example, a client asks that no caregiver of a certain race be assigned) must decline and tell the supervisor. The supervisor explains the agency's policy to the client and documents the conversation.

Employees who believe a client was discriminated against, or who are directed to discriminate, report it immediately to the coordinator or Administrator. Retaliation against anyone who raises a concern is prohibited (see ADM-07).

Clients may file a complaint of discrimination under ADM-09. The coordinator logs it, begins an investigation within 2 business days and informs the client in writing of the outcome. The notice also tells the client that they may file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights and with appropriate New Jersey authorities.

All new employees receive training on this policy at orientation (see PER-06), and all staff are retrained annually (see PER-07), including how to access interpreter services and how to document accommodations.
The coordinator reviews the accommodation log, interpreter use and discrimination complaints at least quarterly and reports trends to the QA committee (see ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the coordinator, funds interpreter and accessibility services, resolves denied accommodation requests and reviews involuntary discharges.
Maintains the interpreter vendor list, accommodation log and complaint file; provides staff training; reports quarterly to QA.
Ask about language and accommodation needs at first contact, arrange interpreters and apply nondiscriminatory assignment criteria.
Evaluates accommodation requests, includes accommodations in the plan of care and confirms effective communication during assessments and supervisory visits.
Treat all clients with respect, use the interpreter service when needed, and report discrimination or accommodation needs to the supervisor.

documentation: Preferred language and accommodation needs on the intake record
Interpreter use record (date, language, interpreter name or vendor ID, mode, purpose)
Client's documented request, if any, to use a family member or friend as interpreter
Accommodation log and decisions, including denial reasons and alternatives offered
Translated vital documents and notice of nondiscrimination
Discrimination complaint file and outcomes
Training attendance records for orientation and annual in-service
Quarterly review summaries submitted to QA

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] CHHAs, nurse supervisors, office staff, volunteers and contractors who work in or have access to a client's home, property or financial information
policies.purpose: To protect clients' property and finances, prevent financial exploitation, and make sure staff understand that they may not accept gifts or money from clients or use client property or accounts.
policies.policy: Caregivers employed by [AGENCY NAME] may not accept gifts, money, loans, tips, bequests or favors from clients or their families. They may not borrow from, sell to or buy from clients. They may not use a client's property, vehicle, credit or debit cards, bank accounts, online accounts or personal identifying information for any reason. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7, CHHAs perform only the tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor, and managing a client's finances is not a delegated task. Orientation covers gifts, money and financial transactions with clients (see PER-06), and the topic is reinforced in annual in-service (see PER-07). Any suspected financial exploitation must be reported under SAF-01. The agency also does not engage in or permit misappropriation of client property.

definitions.definition: The wrongful or unauthorized taking, withholding, use or control of a client's money, property or assets, including by deception, coercion, undue influence or theft.

Anything of value given to a staff member by a client or family member, including cash, checks, jewelry, household items, food beyond a nominal courtesy, tickets, or a promise of inheritance or a change to a will.
Personal belongings, valuables, documents, medications, vehicles, keys, financial instruments and accounts, and any item in the client's home.
Money the client gives a caregiver to buy items specifically listed on the plan of care, with a receipt and change returned to the client.

procedures: At hiring and orientation, each employee receives this policy and signs an acknowledgment that they may not accept gifts or money or use client property or accounts. The signed form is placed in the personnel record (see PER-04 and PER-06).

Orientation and annual in-service include scenarios on gifts, money, loans, requests to be named in a will, requests to use a client's card, and clients who ask for help with banking. Attendance is documented (see PER-07).

The admission packet and service agreement tell clients and families that staff may not accept gifts or money, may not handle bank accounts or cards, and that clients should not offer them (see ADM-12 and CR-01).

At the initial nursing assessment, the RN identifies any risk factors for exploitation, such as dependence on a single person for finances, cognitive impairment, isolation, a recent change in financial control or signs of undue influence. These are documented in the client record and plan of care (see CLN-03 and CLN-04).

Handling money is not a delegated CHHA task. Errands involving client funds are permitted only when listed in the plan of care and the supervising nurse has approved it. The caregiver counts out and records the amount received with the client present. The caregiver obtains an itemized receipt, returns change and the receipt to the client, and has the client initial the entry on the weekly activity record (see CLN-07).

Caregivers do not use client credit or debit cards, checks, ATM cards, PINs or online accounts. If a client asks for such help, the caregiver politely declines and informs the nurse supervisor the same day. The supervisor arranges a safe alternative, such as a family member, a bank service or a representative payee.

Caregivers may not take items from a client's home, including food, medications, supplies, electronics and cash. Caregivers may not store personal items at the client's home. Caregivers do not keep keys to a client's home unless the plan of care and a signed key-release form authorize it. The office logs the keys.

If a client offers a gift, the caregiver declines politely, explaining that agency policy prohibits it. If declining would cause the client significant distress, the caregiver may accept a very small token of nominal value, such as a handwritten card or homemade cookies shared in the client's presence. The caregiver reports it to the supervisor within 1 business day. Cash, gift cards and anything else of value must be declined, and refusing the gift must not be treated as a service issue.

Caregivers report any gift offered or accepted, any request for money, and any client request to be named in a will or to sign documents. They report it to the nurse supervisor within 1 business day. The supervisor records it on the gift log and reviews it with the Administrator.
A caregiver who finds cash, valuables or documents while performing tasks leaves them in place, tells the client or representative, and tells the supervisor.

If a client reports that property is missing, the caregiver does not search the client's belongings. The caregiver tells the supervisor immediately. The supervisor visits or calls the client within 1 business day, helps the client look for the item, and documents the report. If the property cannot be found, the supervisor tells the Administrator. The Administrator completes an incident report (see SAF-02) and decides whether police or other notification is needed.

Any employee or contractor who sees or suspects financial exploitation by anyone, including staff, family members, other providers or strangers, reports it right away to the supervisor or Administrator. They also report to the appropriate authorities under SAF-01. They do not confront the suspected person or investigate on their own.

The Administrator investigates any allegation involving an employee. The employee is removed from the client's case pending the outcome. The agency applies discipline up to termination, reports to the Board of Nursing as required (see ADM-06 and REC-02), and cooperates with law enforcement.
Retaliation against a person who reports suspected exploitation is prohibited and is addressed under ADM-07.
The nurse supervisor reviews the weekly activity records and errand receipts for any client with errand funds at least monthly, and during the 30-day contact and 60-day in-person review (see CLN-08).
The QA committee reviews the gift log, missing-property reports and exploitation allegations at least quarterly (see ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the policy, investigates allegations, makes external reports and applies discipline.
Assesses exploitation risk, approves any errand arrangement, follows up on missing-property reports and reviews the gift log and receipts.
Decline gifts and money, never use client property or accounts, record and report any offer or request, and report suspected exploitation.
Maintain key logs, signed acknowledgments and the gift log, and tell clients about the policy at admission.
Are asked not to offer gifts or money to staff and to tell the agency about any concerns.

documentation: Employee signed acknowledgment of the gift, money and client-property policy
Orientation and in-service attendance records
Plan of care entries for approved errands and exploitation risk
Errand records with receipts and client initials on the weekly activity record
Gift log, key-release forms and key log
Missing-property reports and incident reports
Investigation file, discipline records and any report to authorities
Quarterly QA review summaries

policies.title: Medicaid PCA Certification of Need, Authorization and Limitations
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, nurse supervisors/DON, schedulers, billing staff and CHHAs who serve NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) personal care assistant (PCA) beneficiaries, whether fee-for-service or enrolled in a managed care plan
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] provides Medicaid PCA services only when need has been certified in writing, hours are prior authorized, and the program limitations in N.J.A.C. 10:60 are followed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides Medicaid PCA services only to beneficiaries for whom a physician or practitioner has certified the need for PCA services in writing, at the initial application and annually, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.4. PCA services are provided only within the hours and tasks that are prior authorized. N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8 limits PCA services to a maximum of 40 hours per calendar work week, prior authorized, and unused units cannot be carried over. PCA services provided by a family member are not covered except under the Personal Preference Program (PPP). The fee-for-service PCA rate is $26.68 per hour (code T1019, 15-minute unit), effective July 1, 2024 (NJ SPA 24-0013). Managed care organization (MCO) rates are contracted and are billed under the contract. Person-centered planning and the beneficiary's rights under 42 CFR 441.301(c) are respected in all planning.

definitions.definition: Hands-on assistance with activities of daily living and related household tasks provided to a Medicaid beneficiary in the beneficiary's home, under the direction and supervision of a registered professional nurse.
A written statement by a physician or practitioner that the beneficiary needs PCA services, required at the initial application and annually.
Approval by the State (fee-for-service) or the beneficiary's MCO of the number of PCA hours and units before services are delivered.
A 15-minute billing increment (T1019). Four units equal one hour.
The week used to measure the 40-hour limit. [AGENCY NAME] applies the work week in the authorization and in its payroll records.
A managed care organization that administers NJ FamilyCare benefits, including PCA and MLTSS, for enrolled members.

procedures: At intake for any Medicaid inquiry, the intake coordinator records the beneficiary's NJ FamilyCare ID, program (fee-for-service, MCO plan name, MLTSS or PPP) and the referral source on the intake record (see CLN-01 and CLN-02). The coordinator verifies eligibility and plan enrollment through the State eligibility system or the MCO before scheduling any visit.

Before services begin, the agency obtains a copy of the written physician or practitioner certification of need. The certification must be signed and dated and cover the period of services. If it is missing, expired or unsigned, services do not start. The intake coordinator tells the beneficiary and referral source what is needed and logs the date requested.

The agency tracks the certification's annual due date on the Medicaid tracking log. The DON or designee requests a new certification at least 45 days before the anniversary. If it is not received by the due date, the Administrator notifies the beneficiary and the MCO or State and holds services from the due date until the agency has it, as required by program rules. The agency documents these notices.

The agency obtains and files the written prior authorization showing the authorized hours per week, effective dates and the authorizing entity. For MCO members, the MCO authorizes hours based on the State PCA Assessment tool (see MED-02 and MED-03). The agency never schedules hours beyond what is authorized.
