The scheduler enters the authorized hours and the weekly cap in the scheduling system. The system is set to flag any schedule that would exceed authorized hours for the calendar work week, or exceed 40 PCA hours in a calendar work week for the beneficiary.

The agency does not carry unused units over to later weeks or months. If a beneficiary misses hours, the scheduler offers make-up visits only within the same authorized week. Hours may not be banked and used later. Missed visits are handled under CLN-12.

If a beneficiary needs more hours than authorized, the DON helps the beneficiary or representative ask the MCO or State for a change, supported by the RN reassessment. Hours above the authorization are not delivered under Medicaid unless the authorization is changed in writing. If the beneficiary wants additional hours privately, a separate private-pay service agreement is signed (see ADM-12) and those hours are billed separately and never mixed with Medicaid billing.

Before accepting an assignment, intake staff screen for settings where PCA is not reimbursable. These include assisted living, nursing facilities, hospitals and adult day health during the hours they are provided. If a beneficiary enters one of those settings, services and billing for that period stop (see CLN-14).

Intake staff screen for needs PCA does not cover and tell the referral source when the need falls outside PCA. These include respite, stand-alone supervision, companionship, child care, parenting tasks, mental-health service needs, non-functional diagnoses, acute short-term conditions and needs that are not hands-on. The agency documents the determination and refers the person to the right program (see MED-03).
The agency does not bill Medicaid for PCA if the PCA lives in the beneficiary's home. The scheduler confirms the address of each assigned CHHA against the beneficiary's address before scheduling.

The agency does not assign a family member as PCA under fee-for-service or MCO PCA. This includes a spouse, legal guardian or parent of a minor, for whom no exception is available. If a beneficiary asks for another relative, the Administrator may request a case-by-case exception from the State or the MCO. If an exception is granted in writing, the agency uses the relative only if that person is currently certified as a homemaker-home health aide, is an employee of [AGENCY NAME], and is directly supervised by [AGENCY NAME]'s RN. If the beneficiary wants a family member paid, the agency explains that the Personal Preference Program is the program that covers it (see MED-03).

When two or more beneficiaries live in the same residence, the nurse supervisor and scheduler combine each beneficiary's individual hands-on hours with group hours for household tasks as the authorization allows. Time is allocated and recorded so no task or hour is billed twice.

Billing staff bill Medicaid at the fee-for-service rate of $26.68 per hour ($6.67 per 15-minute unit, rounded per State billing instructions) or at the rate in the MCO contract. They bill only electronically verified visits that match authorized units and the signed plan of care (see CLN-12 and MED-03). The billing supervisor reviews the MCO contract rate sheet each year and when the State changes the rate. The rate is confirmed against the current State plan and fee schedule.

The Administrator or billing supervisor audits 10 percent of Medicaid PCA claims monthly against authorization, certification, EVV data and weekly activity records. Overpayments are reported and refunded as required, and corrective action is documented (see ADM-06).
The Medicaid tracking log, with certification and authorization dates for each beneficiary, is reviewed weekly by the DON or designee and monthly by the Administrator.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures compliance with Medicaid PCA rules, approves relative-exception requests, oversees claims audits and refunds.
Confirms certification and authorization before the start of service, tracks annual recertification, supports requests for hours changes and screens for non-covered needs.
Verifies eligibility, obtains certification and authorization, and screens for settings and need types that are excluded.
Schedules only authorized hours, enforces the 40-hour weekly cap, does not carry over units, and checks for live-in and family-member conflicts.
Bill only verified, authorized visits at the correct rate and keep the audit trail.

documentation: Written physician/practitioner certification of need (initial and annual)
Written prior authorization from the State or MCO showing hours, units and dates
Medicaid tracking log with certification and authorization dates
Intake record with eligibility verification and program type
Weekly schedule and authorization reconciliation
Written exceptions and approvals for relative PCAs, if any
Private-pay agreements for any hours beyond the authorization
Billing records, rate sheets and monthly audit results

policies.title: Medicaid PCA RN Assessment and Supervision
policies.applies_to: RN supervisors, the DON, schedulers and CHHAs working as PCAs for NJ FamilyCare beneficiaries
policies.purpose: To make sure every Medicaid PCA beneficiary has a timely RN assessment and a written plan of care, and that the RN directly supervises the PCA in the home as required by N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5.
policies.policy: A registered professional nurse (RN) employed or contracted by [AGENCY NAME] assesses each Medicaid PCA beneficiary and prepares the plan of care, consistent with the physician/practitioner certification, at the start of service and never later than 48 hours after it begins. The plan lists tasks, hours, goals and the beneficiary's strengths and family needs. It is dated and signed by the PCA and the RN. The RN directly supervises the PCA in the home during the PCA's assigned time. The first supervisory visit is initiated within 48 hours of the start of service, and visits continue at least once every 60 days. Additional visits are made for a new PCA, nurse delegation or changed needs. For beneficiaries enrolled in a managed care plan, the plan completes the State PCA Assessment tool and authorizes hours. [AGENCY NAME]'s RN completes the agency's own assessment and plan of care and does not change the MCO's authorized hours.

definitions.definition: An in-person nursing evaluation of the beneficiary's functional status, health needs, home safety, strengths, family needs and supports, used to prepare the plan of care.
The written plan listing tasks, hours, goals and the beneficiary's strengths and family needs, signed and dated by the PCA and the RN.
The RN's on-site observation and oversight of the PCA delivering care in the beneficiary's home during the PCA's assigned time.
The standardized assessment completed by the managed care plan for its members to determine PCA need and authorized hours.

procedures: When a Medicaid PCA referral is accepted and the certification and authorization are in hand (see MED-01), the DON assigns an RN and records the planned start-of-service date and the 48-hour deadline on the Medicaid tracking log.

The RN completes the in-person assessment in the beneficiary's home at the start of service. It must be completed no later than 48 hours after services begin. The RN uses the assessment form in CLN-03 and documents the date and time. If the RN cannot meet the deadline, the DON informs the Administrator immediately. The agency does not delay the assessment for scheduling convenience.

The RN confirms that the assessment findings are consistent with the physician/practitioner certification. If they are not, the RN contacts the practitioner, documents the discussion and does not finalize the plan until the difference is resolved.

For MCO members, the RN obtains the MCO's State PCA Assessment tool results and authorization. The agency does not complete the State tool in place of the MCO and does not set hours for MCO members. If the RN finds the beneficiary's needs differ from the authorization, the RN documents the findings and the DON asks the MCO for reassessment (see MED-03).

The RN prepares the plan of care listing tasks, authorized hours, goals, the beneficiary's strengths and family needs (see CLN-04). Tasks for the PCA must be within what the PCA is permitted to do and within the authorized scope (see CLN-10).

The plan of care is dated and signed by the RN and the PCA. The beneficiary or representative receives a copy, and the original is placed in the client record (see CLN-04 and REC-01). Services are provided only according to the signed plan.

The RN initiates the first direct supervisory visit to the home within 48 hours of the start of service, during the PCA's assigned time. The RN observes the PCA performing care, confirms competency in each assigned task (see CLN-06), and reviews the plan with the PCA and beneficiary.

The RN makes subsequent in-home supervisory visits at least once every 60 days while services continue. The DON sets the next due date on the tracking log at each visit. A visit that is more than 60 days after the prior one is a deficiency and must be reported to the Administrator.

The RN makes additional visits in the following situations: a new PCA is assigned; the RN delegates a nursing task to the PCA (see CLN-05); or the beneficiary's needs change, for example after a hospitalization, a fall or a change in condition (see CLN-13). The reason is documented in the visit note.

When more than one PCA serves a beneficiary, the RN rotates supervisory visits across the PCAs and shifts until all PCAs have been assessed on each covered shift. The DON keeps a rotation schedule showing the PCA, shift and date of each observation.

At each visit, the RN observes personal care, infection control, safe transfer technique and communication, and asks the beneficiary about satisfaction and any concerns. The RN talks privately with the beneficiary and family, and reviews the weekly activity records (see CLN-07).

If the RN finds a performance problem, the RN gives the PCA immediate coaching, documents it, and arranges a competency re-check within 14 days. For safety concerns, the RN removes the PCA from the assignment and notifies the DON and Administrator right away (see CLN-09 and SAF-02).

If the beneficiary's condition changes, the RN updates the plan of care, signs and dates it, and has the PCA sign it. If the change requires more hours or different services, the RN follows MED-03 to request reassessment by the MCO or State.

The RN documents every visit in the client record on the same day, including the date and time, the PCA observed, tasks observed, findings, teaching, actions taken and the next due date. Notes are signed with the RN's name and credentials.

Every month, the DON reviews the Medicaid tracking log for assessments completed within 48 hours, supervisory visits within 48 hours and every 60 days, and signed and dated plans. Results are reported to the Administrator and the QA committee (see ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Assigns RNs, tracks the 48-hour and 60-day deadlines, rotates visits among multiple PCAs and reports missed deadlines to the Administrator.
Performs the assessment, writes and signs the plan of care, supervises the PCA in the home and documents each visit.
Signs and follows the plan of care, performs only assigned tasks, and tells the RN about any change in the beneficiary.
Schedules the RN visit within the required timeframe and coordinates with the PCA's shifts.
Ensures sufficient RN staffing, reviews monthly compliance reports and acts on any deficiency.

documentation: RN assessment dated within 48 hours of the start of service
Plan of care listing tasks, hours, goals, strengths and family needs, dated and signed by the RN and PCA
State PCA Assessment tool results and MCO authorization (MCO members)
Supervisory visit notes with date, time and PCA observed
Rotation schedule for multiple PCAs and shifts
Medicaid tracking log of deadlines
Documentation of additional visits and their reasons
Monthly compliance reports and QA minutes

policies.title: Coordination with NJ FamilyCare, MLTSS and the Personal Preference Program
policies.applies_to: Administrator, DON, intake coordinators, schedulers, billing staff and care coordinators involved with NJ FamilyCare, MLTSS and Personal Preference Program (PPP) clients
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] coordinates properly with NJ FamilyCare managed care organizations (MCOs), county Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) offices and other program entities, confirms authorization before starting services, uses electronic visit verification (EVV), and understands how the Personal Preference Program differs from agency-delivered PCA.
policies.policy: Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) is delivered through NJ FamilyCare MCOs, and the county Area Agency on Aging ADRC handles intake and screening for adults 21 and older who seek MLTSS. [AGENCY NAME] confirms MCO or State authorization in writing before starting any Medicaid-funded service. The Personal Preference Program (PPP) is a self-directed program in which the participant directs the services and hires their own workers. Payment for self-directed PCA follows the methodology in NJ SPA 22-0005. [AGENCY NAME] does not act as the employer of PPP workers and does not bill for PPP services unless a written agreement with the program entity assigns that role. Fee-for-service PCA is paid at the rate in NJ SPA 24-0013, which is $26.68 per hour effective July 1, 2024. MCO rates are set by contract. Electronic visit verification is required for Medicaid personal care services delivered in the home under Section 12006(a) of the 21st Century Cures Act (42 USC 1396b(l)). [AGENCY NAME] uses the State's designated EVV system, HHAeXchange. All planning respects the beneficiary's person-centered rights under 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: New Jersey's Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program, administered by the Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services (DMAHS) in the Department of Human Services.
Managed Long Term Services and Supports, the NJ FamilyCare program that provides home and community-based services and nursing facility care through MCOs.
The county Aging and Disability Resource Connection, which provides information, intake and screening for adults 21 and older seeking MLTSS.
A managed care organization contracted by the State to administer NJ FamilyCare benefits and authorize services for its members.
A self-directed Medicaid personal care program in which the participant manages a budget, selects and directs their own workers, and may employ family members, subject to program rules.
Electronic visit verification: an electronic system that verifies the type of service, the person served, the date, the location, the worker and the start and end times of each visit.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a current list of the MCOs with which [AGENCY NAME] is contracted, with provider contacts, contract effective dates, credentialing status and billing instructions. The list is updated whenever a contract changes and is reviewed quarterly.

At intake, the intake coordinator identifies the program (fee-for-service PCA, MCO PCA, MLTSS, PPP or private pay) and records the NJ FamilyCare ID, MCO name and care manager name and phone on the intake record (see CLN-02).

If an inquirer is an adult 21 or older who may need MLTSS and is not yet enrolled, the intake coordinator refers them to the county ADRC for screening and gives the ADRC contact. The referral is documented. The agency does not state or promise eligibility.

For MLTSS and other MCO members, the intake coordinator obtains the MCO's written authorization (services, hours, dates and authorization number) and the care manager's contact information before the first visit. Services do not start without the written authorization. If a referral is urgent, the Administrator may start services only if the MCO gives written or recorded confirmation of authorization.

The intake coordinator confirms that the authorization matches the physician/practitioner certification (see MED-01) and the services requested. Differences are resolved with the care manager before the start of service.

The DON or RN supervisor contacts the care manager within 2 business days of the start of service to confirm the start date and the assigned caregiver, and shares the plan of care consistent with the MCO's care plan (see MED-02 and CLN-04).

The DON notifies the care manager within 1 business day of any significant change in condition, hospitalization, emergency, incident, missed visit pattern, caregiver change or client refusal of services. The notice is documented in the client record (see CLN-13 and SAF-02).

The agency attends or provides input to care planning meetings at the care manager's request. The beneficiary's choices and goals are recorded and followed. The agency makes sure the beneficiary knows they may choose among providers and may make complaints without retaliation (see CR-01 and ADM-09).

If a beneficiary asks about self-directing services or paying a family member, the intake coordinator explains that PPP is a separate self-directed program. Under PPP, the participant directs their own services and can hire workers, including some family members. The coordinator gives the person the contact for the County ADRC or MCO care manager, and documents the referral. The agency does not enroll participants in PPP.

For any participant who moves to PPP, the DON coordinates the transition with the participant and care manager so that care is not interrupted. The agency continues services until the transition date or the end of the authorization and follows CLN-14.

If [AGENCY NAME] has a written agreement to provide services to a PPP participant, the Administrator ensures that billing follows the payment methodology in NJ SPA 22-0005 and the agreement. The agency does not use agency rates to bill PPP, and does not make PPP workers its employees unless they are hired as agency staff under separate terms.

EVV: The agency uses the State's EVV system, HHAeXchange, for all Medicaid personal care visits delivered in the home. The Administrator makes sure each CHHA is trained at orientation and before the first Medicaid visit, and each CHHA is registered in the system (see CLN-12).

At every visit, the caregiver records the start and end of the visit electronically at the client's home, and does not use a device belonging to the client unless the system allows it. When EVV cannot be used (device or network failure), the caregiver telephones the office. The scheduler documents a manual edit with the reason, the supervisor's approval and the corrective plan. Manual edits are reviewed weekly for patterns.

Billing staff submit claims only for visits that match an authorization and EVV record. The EVV data must show the correct member, service, caregiver, date and times. Claims that do not match are held and corrected before submission, and billing staff do not alter records to match.

Billing staff bill fee-for-service PCA at the rate in NJ SPA 24-0013 ($26.68 per hour, T1019, 15-minute unit, effective July 1, 2024) and bill MCOs at the contracted rate. The billing supervisor confirms rates every July and whenever the State or an MCO announces a change.

The DON and billing supervisor reconcile authorizations, EVV and billing monthly for each Medicaid client. Variances are reported to the Administrator, who documents corrective action. Overpayments are reported and repaid as required (see ADM-06).
The Administrator reviews MCO notices, State provider bulletins and program changes at least monthly. Changes that affect policy are brought to the QA committee within 30 days (see ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains MCO contracts, EVV compliance, state program updates and corrective action for billing variances.
Coordinates with care managers, shares plans of care, reports changes in condition and manages transitions.
Identifies the program, refers to ADRC where appropriate, obtains and verifies written authorization before the start of service.
Schedules to authorized hours, supports EVV use and approves and documents manual edits.
Bill only authorized, verified visits at the correct rate and reconcile monthly.
Use EVV correctly at every visit, follow the plan of care and report changes to the supervisor.

documentation: List of contracted MCOs and contacts
Written MCO or State authorization before the start of service
Intake record showing program type, NJ FamilyCare ID and care manager
ADRC and PPP referral records
Care manager communication log
EVV records, manual edit log with reasons and approvals
Billing reconciliation and audit reports
Rate confirmation records and written agreements with program entities

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, CHHAs, nurse supervisors, contractors and volunteers
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and exploitation of clients, to require prompt reporting of suspected abuse to the agency and the proper New Jersey authority, and to protect people who report.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect and exploitation of clients, whether by staff, family, other caregivers or anyone else. Child abuse, elder abuse and domestic violence are topics in orientation and in annual in-service training (see PER-06 and PER-07). Any employee who suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation reports it right away to the agency and to the proper New Jersey authority. Reporting to the agency does not replace the legal duty to report to the authorities. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7, CHHAs perform only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor and employed CHHAs are the only aides the agency places, so staff are known to the agency and their tasks are defined and documented. Staff are protected from retaliation for reporting in good faith. This policy supports each client's right to be free from abuse and to be treated with dignity under 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: Willful infliction of physical harm, pain, injury, sexual contact without consent, emotional or psychological harm, or unreasonable confinement.
Failure by a caregiver or other responsible person to provide the care, goods or services necessary to maintain a client's health and safety, including self-neglect.
The wrongful use of a client's money, property, identity or resources for another person's benefit (see CR-03).
A pattern of abusive behavior by a current or former partner or household or family member that is used to control or harm another person.
The county-based program that investigates reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults living in the community.
The New Jersey Department of Children and Families hotline for reporting suspected child abuse or neglect.

procedures: At hiring, each employee receives this policy and signs an acknowledgment that they understand their duty to report. Orientation covers recognizing child abuse, elder abuse and domestic violence, the reporting steps and retaliation protections. Attendance is recorded (see PER-06). The same topics are repeated each year in annual in-service (see PER-07).

Before assignment, the agency screens employees under PER-10. CHHAs are verified as actively certified and employed by [AGENCY NAME] (see PER-03 and ADM-04). Caregivers perform only tasks in the plan of care delegated by the supervisor, and any request to do other things is reported to the supervisor.

The RN assessment screens each client for risk of abuse, neglect and exploitation, and for signs of domestic violence. Findings are recorded in the client record and plan of care (see CLN-03 and CLN-04).

Staff learn the signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation, such as unexplained injuries, fear of a person, sudden changes in behavior or finances, poor hygiene, unsafe living conditions, missing property and isolation.
If anyone is in immediate danger, the employee calls 911 first, then notifies the supervisor.

For suspected abuse or neglect of a child (anyone under 18), the employee reports immediately to the New Jersey DCF child abuse hotline, 1-877-652-2873 (1-877-NJ ABUSE) [verify before publishing]. New Jersey law requires any person who has reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected to report. The employee does not wait for supervisor approval and does not need proof.

For suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of an adult, the employee reports to the county Adult Protective Services intake at [COUNTY APS INTAKE NUMBER] [verify before publishing]. The agency keeps a list of the intake number for each county it serves at the front desk and in each caregiver's service guide.

For suspected domestic violence, the employee tells the supervisor and, with the client's consent where the client is a competent adult, helps the client reach a domestic violence program or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. Where a child or vulnerable adult is at risk, the reporting rules in steps 6 and 7 apply regardless of consent.

The employee also tells the nurse supervisor or Administrator at [PHONE] as soon as possible and no later than the end of the shift. Outside business hours, the employee uses the on-call number (see ADM-11). The employee does not investigate or confront the suspected person, and does not promise the client confidentiality.

The supervisor completes an incident report the same day (see SAF-02). The report records who, what, when, where, what was seen or said, injuries, the reports made (agency, hotline, APS, police) and times, and the names of those contacted.

The Administrator confirms within 24 hours that the proper authority has been notified. If the employee has not reported, the Administrator reports directly. The Administrator assigns a nurse to visit the client within 24 hours (sooner if risk is high) to assess safety and update the plan of care.

When the suspected person is an agency employee, the Administrator immediately removes the person from client contact pending investigation, tells the client's representative and care manager as appropriate, and cooperates fully with the investigating authorities. The Administrator reports to the Board of Nursing for CHHAs where required and applies discipline up to termination (see ADM-06 and REC-02). Substantiated findings are recorded in the personnel file and in the registry check systems as required (see PER-10).

When the suspected person is a family member or other provider, the nurse supervisor works with the authorities and the Medicaid care manager, if any, on a safety plan. This may include changing the schedule, adding supervision visits or, if the home is unsafe, arranging discharge or transfer under CLN-14.

The agency does not retaliate against any person who reports suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation in good faith. Retaliation is a serious violation and results in discipline up to termination. Employees who experience or see retaliation report it to the Administrator or use the process in ADM-07.

The agency protects the confidentiality of the reporter and the client to the extent allowed by law. Information is shared only with the authorities, the care manager and those who need it to protect the client, consistent with ADM-10.

The Administrator keeps a log of all suspected abuse, neglect and exploitation reports, the authorities notified and the outcomes. The QA committee reviews the log quarterly for patterns and training needs (see ADM-14).
The Administrator checks hotline and APS numbers every year and whenever notified of a change. The Administrator updates orientation materials, caregiver guides and postings within 10 business days.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures reports are made, removes accused staff, reports to the Board of Nursing and other authorities, applies discipline and keeps the log.
Screens for risk, visits the client within 24 hours of a report, completes the incident report and updates the plan of care.
Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately to the proper authority and to the agency, and never retaliate.
Provides orientation and annual training, collects acknowledgments and keeps the hotline and APS numbers current.
Reviews reports and trends quarterly and recommends prevention measures.

documentation: Employee signed acknowledgment of the reporting policy
Orientation and annual in-service attendance records on child abuse, elder abuse and domestic violence
Client risk screening in the assessment and plan of care
Incident reports with times and the authorities contacted
Log of abuse, neglect and exploitation reports and outcomes
Investigation records, discipline records and reports to the Board of Nursing or other authorities
Updated DCF hotline and county APS numbers and posting dates
Quarterly QA review summaries

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All CHHAs, Nurse Supervisors/Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, office staff and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME], for all clients (NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS, Personal Preference Program and private-pay)
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident involving a client, caregiver or the agency is reported at once, documented, acted on and reviewed, so that client safety is protected and the plan of care is revised when needed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every staff member to report any incident to the Nurse Supervisor immediately and to follow the verbal report with a written incident report. Any change in a client's condition is reported as set out in the client's plan of care. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9 (C9), when a plan of care needs revision a licensed person must reassess it immediately, and when the plan is not being carried out properly the agency must take corrective action immediately. Incidents that show either problem are handled under those requirements. All incidents are reviewed in the Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program (see ADM-14). Incident reports are confidential and are not placed in a way that exposes them to unauthorized people. No staff member will be retaliated against for reporting an incident (see ADM-07).

definitions.definition: Any unplanned or unusual event that causes or could cause harm or distress to a client, caregiver or other person, or that involves damage to property. Examples are falls, injuries, medication errors or refusals, elective or emergency transport to a hospital, a death, a missing or wandering client, suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, property loss or damage, an exposure to blood or body fluids, a workplace injury or assault, a missed visit that puts a client at risk, and a complaint alleging harm.
A noticeable change in a client's physical, mental, emotional or functional status, home environment or support system that differs from the plan of care.

An incident that must also be reported outside the agency, such as to law enforcement, Adult Protective Services, a payer, a Managed Care Organization (MCO) or the Division of Consumer Affairs. External reporting is governed by SAF-01 and REC-02.

procedures: The caregiver first ensures the immediate safety of the client and self. If there is an emergency, the caregiver calls 911 and then follows CLN-13.

The caregiver notifies the Nurse Supervisor immediately, by phone, at [PHONE] during business hours or the on-call number [ON-CALL PHONE] after hours (see ADM-11). A text or email alone does not meet this step.
If the Nurse Supervisor cannot be reached within 15 minutes, the caregiver calls the on-call line again and then the Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], at [PHONE], and documents each attempt.

The Nurse Supervisor gives the caregiver direction, decides whether the client needs urgent medical attention, and decides whether the physician, practitioner, family or representative, the case manager or the MCO care manager must be told.

The caregiver completes the written Incident Report form as soon as possible and no later than the end of the shift in which the incident occurred. The report states facts only: date, time, place, who was involved, what was seen and heard, actions taken, who was notified and when.
The caregiver signs and dates the report and gives it to the Nurse Supervisor. The caregiver does not keep copies at home or share the report with anyone outside the agency.
The Nurse Supervisor reviews the report within one business day, adds a clinical follow-up note, and records any contact with the client, family, practitioner or payer.

If the incident shows a change in the client's condition, the Nurse Supervisor reviews the plan of care. Where it needs revision, a licensed person reassesses it immediately in accordance with N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9 (C9) (see CLN-04 and CLN-08).

If the incident shows that the plan of care is not being carried out properly, the Nurse Supervisor takes corrective action immediately, such as retraining, re-demonstrating competency, reassigning the caregiver or adjusting the schedule. The action is documented (see CLN-06 and CLN-09).
Incidents involving suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or a client death are also reported to the Administrator the same day, and the reporting steps in SAF-01 are followed.
Incidents involving a caregiver's injury or exposure to blood or body fluids are also handled under SAF-03 and SAF-05, and the Administrator is told the same day.
The Administrator decides within one business day whether the incident is reportable to an outside agency and makes those reports, and documents the decision (see ADM-06 and REC-02).

The Nurse Supervisor files the original incident report in the incident log, keeps a copy of any information about the client in the client record (clinical facts only), and enters the incident in the incident log with a tracking number.

The Administrator and DON/HCSS review the incident log at least quarterly in the QAPI meeting. They look for trends by caregiver, client, time and type of event, set corrective actions with owners and due dates, and record the results in the QAPI minutes (see ADM-14).
The Nurse Supervisor tells the client or representative the result of the review, as appropriate, and records that conversation.

responsibilities.duty: Secures safety, reports immediately to the Nurse Supervisor, completes the written report by the end of the shift, and reports changes in condition as stated in the plan of care.

responsibilities.role: Nurse Supervisor / Health Care Practitioner Supervisor
responsibilities.duty: Receives reports, directs the response, reviews each report within one business day, reassesses or revises the plan of care and takes corrective action immediately when needed, and keeps the incident log.
Decides on external reporting, ensures the policy is followed, and ensures no retaliation.
Review incident trends at least quarterly and track corrective actions to completion.

documentation: Incident Report form, signed and dated by the caregiver and reviewed by the Nurse Supervisor
Incident log with tracking numbers
Client record entry of clinical facts, notifications and plan-of-care changes
Corrective action documentation (retraining, competency re-checks, reassignment)
External reports and the Administrator's reportability decision
QAPI meeting minutes showing incident review

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All CHHAs, Nurse Supervisors, office staff who enter client homes, and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from infection and from exposure to blood-borne pathogens by training staff, providing protective equipment and vaccination, and setting clear steps for standard precautions, needle sticks and exposure follow-up.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows standard precautions in every client home and complies with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). Infection control, blood-borne pathogens, standard precautions and needle-stick response are covered at orientation (see PER-06) and at the annual mandatory in-service (see PER-07). The agency offers the hepatitis B vaccine and provides personal protective equipment (PPE) at no cost to employees. Each employee's TB screening and immunity documentation is kept in the personnel record (see PER-05 and PER-04). Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7 (C8), a CHHA may perform only tasks delegated by, or directed by, the health care practitioner supervisor, who must ensure the CHHA demonstrates competence in each task and document every delegated task in the patient record. Infection-control-related tasks, such as handling soiled linens, cleaning up body fluids, or any task involving a client's wound, catheter or ostomy equipment, are performed by a CHHA only if the supervisor has delegated the task, confirmed competence and recorded the delegation.

definitions.definition: Infection-prevention practices applied to all clients regardless of diagnosis, including hand hygiene, use of PPE, safe handling of sharps and soiled items, respiratory hygiene and environmental cleaning.
Microorganisms in human blood or other potentially infectious materials that can cause disease, including hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus and HIV.

A specific eye, mouth, other mucous-membrane, non-intact skin or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious material that results from performing an employee's duties, including a needle-stick or sharps injury.
Gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection and similar items worn to prevent contact with infectious material.
The written plan required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 that identifies employees with occupational exposure risk and describes how exposure is prevented and handled.

procedures: The Administrator and DON/HCSS maintain a written Exposure Control Plan, review it at least annually and update it when tasks, procedures or technology change. The plan is available to every employee.

At orientation, before the first client assignment, each new CHHA completes training on infection control, blood-borne pathogens, standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE use and needle-stick response, and the training is documented (see PER-06).

The same topics are repeated at the annual mandatory in-service, at least once every 12 months, and whenever new tasks or hazards are introduced. Training records include date, content, trainer and attendee signatures (see PER-07).

The agency offers the hepatitis B vaccine series at no cost to every employee with occupational exposure risk, within 10 working days of initial assignment. An employee who declines signs a declination statement and may accept the vaccine later at no cost.

Before a CHHA's first assignment, the agency obtains the employee health attestation and TB screening and immunity results and places them in the personnel record (see PER-05). The Administrator tracks due dates for repeat screening.
The agency supplies PPE and hand-hygiene supplies at no cost. CHHAs carry gloves, hand sanitizer and other needed PPE to each visit and request replacements from the office when low.

In each home the CHHA practices hand hygiene before and after client contact, after removing gloves, and before preparing food. The CHHA wears gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin or soiled items and changes gloves between tasks.

CHHAs do not perform sterile procedures or any task involving sharps, wounds, catheters, ostomies or similar care unless the supervisor has delegated the task and confirmed competence under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7 (C8). The supervisor records each delegation in the patient record.

CHHAs do not recap, bend or break used needles and do not handle a client's sharps except to move a sharps container as instructed. Used sharps are kept in the client's puncture-resistant container, and the CHHA alerts the Nurse Supervisor if no container is available.
CHHAs bag soiled linens and waste, handle laundry with gloves, clean and disinfect surfaces and equipment as instructed, and dispose of waste as directed in the plan of care.

A CHHA who has a fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a rash, a respiratory illness or another communicable condition notifies the office before the shift and does not enter a client home until cleared by the Nurse Supervisor.

The CHHA tells the Nurse Supervisor when a client shows signs of an infection or communicable disease, such as fever, new cough, wound drainage, rash or diarrhea, and the Nurse Supervisor follows CLN-13.

After any needle-stick, sharps injury or other exposure incident, the employee immediately washes the area with soap and water (or flushes eyes or mucous membranes with water), then notifies the Nurse Supervisor at once.

The Nurse Supervisor arranges a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up for the employee, at no cost, immediately and in any case on the same day, and provides the required exposure information to the health care professional. The employee completes an incident report (see SAF-02) and the agency records the event on its sharps injury log.

The Administrator keeps employee medical records related to exposure and vaccination confidential and separate from the general personnel file, and retains them for the period required by OSHA. Training records are kept for at least three years.
Infection incidents, exposure incidents and training completion rates are reviewed in the QAPI program at least quarterly (see ADM-14).

responsibilities.duty: Follows standard precautions, uses PPE, reports illness and exposures at once, and performs only tasks that have been delegated.

responsibilities.role: Nurse Supervisor / Health Care Practitioner Supervisor
responsibilities.duty: Delegates infection-control-related tasks, confirms competence, records delegation, directs exposure follow-up and guides the response to infection in clients.

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All CHHAs, Nurse Supervisors, scheduling and office staff and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has a documented emergency plan, staff know what to do in an emergency, and the agency can continue to serve clients during severe weather, power outages, public-health emergencies and other disasters.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] records an emergency plan for each client in the in-person assessment (see CLN-03). Emergency procedures are a required orientation topic (see PER-06). The agency also maintains an agency-wide continuity and disaster plan so that care continues, or clients are safely handed off, during a disaster. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7 (C8), a CHHA performs only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor, and an emergency plan does not authorize a CHHA to perform clinical tasks beyond the delegation. In an emergency a CHHA's role is to call for help, keep the client safe, notify the agency and follow the written plan.

definitions.definition: A written plan, recorded in the in-person assessment, that lists emergency contacts, the client's address and directions, medical conditions and medication list, preferred hospital, mobility and evacuation needs, the location of equipment such as oxygen, and who will help in a disaster.
The agency-wide plan for maintaining or restoring services during an event such as severe storms, flooding, extreme heat or cold, power or phone outages, a pandemic or loss of the office.

A client who would face serious harm if a visit were missed or delayed, for example because of dependence on oxygen or powered equipment, inability to evacuate without help, or living alone with cognitive impairment.

procedures: During the in-person nursing assessment, the nurse completes the emergency section: emergency contacts, preferred hospital, physician or practitioner, medical conditions, medication and allergy list, mobility and evacuation needs, equipment that depends on electricity or oxygen, pets and the person who will help in a disaster (see CLN-03).

The nurse rates the client as high-risk or standard risk for disasters and records the rating in the plan of care. The emergency plan is reviewed at the 60-day in-person re-evaluation and whenever the client's condition or living situation changes (see CLN-08).

The CHHA is given the client's emergency information before the first visit and reviews it with the client at the first visit. A copy is kept in the client's home where the client agrees, and the agency keeps the original in the record.

At orientation each CHHA is trained on emergency procedures: calling 911, responding to falls, choking, fire, loss of consciousness, a suspected stroke or heart attack, severe weather and evacuation, and when to call the Nurse Supervisor (see PER-06).

In a life-threatening emergency, the CHHA calls 911 first, stays with the client, gives only the help the CHHA is trained and delegated to give, and then notifies the Nurse Supervisor and the client's emergency contact. The steps in CLN-13 and SAF-02 are followed.

The Administrator maintains a written agency continuity and disaster plan that covers: loss of the office or phone and computer systems, a backup way to reach staff and clients, protection and backup of electronic records, staff shortages, vehicle and fuel problems, and public-health emergencies.
The Administrator, with the Nurse Supervisor, keeps a current list of high-risk clients ranked by need for visits during a disaster, with each client's emergency contacts and phone numbers.

When a storm or other event is forecast, the Nurse Supervisor and scheduler call high-risk clients and their representatives before the event, confirm their plan, and arrange the schedule so that high-risk clients are visited first. Staff are told which clients to prioritize.

If a CHHA cannot reach a client's home because of a disaster, the CHHA notifies the scheduler immediately. The Nurse Supervisor then telephones the client, arranges a replacement caregiver or family help, asks for a welfare check by [LOCAL POLICE OR 911] when a high-risk client cannot be reached, and documents the efforts (see CLN-12).

A CHHA never leaves a client who is in immediate danger. If an evacuation is ordered, the CHHA helps the client follow the emergency plan, notifies the Nurse Supervisor and records where the client has gone.

For public-health emergencies, the Administrator follows current guidance from the New Jersey Department of Health and local health departments and updates infection-control and staffing procedures (see SAF-03).
The agency tells payers, MCO care managers and Personal Preference Program case managers when services cannot be delivered because of a disaster, in line with their requirements (see MED-03).

After any emergency or disaster the Nurse Supervisor reviews each affected client's condition and plan of care, and the Administrator holds a debrief within 14 days. The results are given to the QAPI Committee (see ADM-14).
The Administrator reviews and updates the agency continuity and disaster plan at least annually, tests the staff call tree at least annually, and records the date and results.

policies.title: Caregiver Safety, Workplace Violence and Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All CHHAs, Nurse Supervisors, office staff who enter client homes, and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from injury, violence and unsafe conditions in client homes, and to control the risks of driving clients, so that care can be delivered safely.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a workplace free from recognized hazards, consistent with the OSHA General Duty Clause, and protects employees from blood-borne pathogen exposure under 29 CFR 1910.1030 (see SAF-03). Employee safety and back safety are required annual in-service topics (see PER-07). A home safety and fall-risk review is part of every assessment (see CLN-03). Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7 (C8), a CHHA performs only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor, and the supervisor ensures competence in each task, including safe lifting and transfers. Clients are transported in a caregiver's or agency vehicle only with written agency approval, and only by a caregiver who has a valid driver's license and the required insurance. The agency does not allow retaliation against an employee who raises a safety concern or leaves an unsafe situation.

definitions.definition: Any threat or act of physical violence, harassment, intimidation, sexual harassment or other threatening behavior directed at an employee by a client, family member, visitor, co-worker or other person.
Use of correct body mechanics, gait belts, lifts and other devices, and help from another person, when moving or repositioning a client, so as to reduce injury to the caregiver and client.
Driving a client in a vehicle for errands, appointments or other purposes, whether the vehicle is owned by the caregiver, the client or the agency.
A signed agency authorization, kept on file, that allows a named caregiver to transport a named client under stated conditions.

procedures: During the in-person assessment, the nurse reviews the home for hazards and fall risk, including clutter, poor lighting, loose rugs, stairs, bathroom safety, working smoke alarms, pets, weapons, smoking, oxygen use and other hazards to caregivers. Findings and the plan to reduce risks are recorded (see CLN-03).

The nurse also records known risks to caregivers, such as a history of aggression, unsafe neighborhoods, lack of lighting or isolated locations, and tells the assigned CHHA before the first visit. Information is shared only as needed and with respect for client privacy.

At orientation and every year in the annual in-service, each CHHA is trained on employee safety, back safety and safe lifting, workplace violence prevention and de-escalation, and personal safety when traveling to and from client homes (see PER-06 and PER-07).

Before a CHHA performs a transfer or other lifting task, the Nurse Supervisor confirms that the task is in the plan of care and delegated, and the CHHA demonstrates competence (see CLN-05 and CLN-06). The CHHA uses a gait belt or equipment where available and asks for a second person when needed. A CHHA does not lift a client alone if it is unsafe.

A CHHA who is threatened, harassed or hurt by a client, family member or other person leaves the situation if it is unsafe, calls 911 if in danger, and notifies the Nurse Supervisor at once. The CHHA completes an incident report by the end of the shift (see SAF-02).

The Nurse Supervisor contacts the CHHA promptly, arranges medical care, decides whether to suspend visits to the home, assigns a second person or ends the service, and tells the Administrator the same day. Where a client or family member's conduct is the problem, the Nurse Supervisor follows CLN-14 for any discontinuation.

The Administrator reports any crime to law enforcement as appropriate, supports the employee in filing any report, and records the follow-up. Threats and violence incidents are reviewed in QAPI (see ADM-14).

A CHHA who has experienced sexual harassment or other conduct by a client or co-worker may report it to the Nurse Supervisor, the Administrator or the compliance contact without fear of retaliation (see ADM-06 and ADM-07).

Work-related injuries are reported to the Nurse Supervisor immediately. The agency provides first aid or sends the employee for medical care, completes an incident report and notifies the workers' compensation carrier on the day of the injury.

CHHAs tell the office their schedule and location, keep their phones charged and available, and call the office if they feel unsafe, are delayed or cannot enter the home. The office checks on a CHHA who does not report for a visit or whom it cannot reach.

Transport of clients is not part of a CHHA's duties unless the plan of care includes it and the Administrator or Nurse Supervisor gives written approval before the first trip. The approval names the caregiver and client, the allowed purposes and the vehicle.

Before approving transport, the Administrator checks that the CHHA holds a valid New Jersey or other state driver's license, the vehicle is registered and insured, and the insurance covers business use or client transport. Copies of the license and proof of insurance are placed in the personnel record and updated at each renewal.

A CHHA who transports a client uses seat belts for all passengers, does not use a handheld phone while driving, does not transport a client who needs a wheelchair-accessible vehicle or other equipment the CHHA cannot safely handle, and does not transport when impaired or unwell.
If a client's condition makes transport unsafe, the CHHA does not drive. In an emergency the CHHA calls 911 rather than driving the client to a hospital.
If a CHHA is in a vehicle collision with a client aboard, the CHHA calls 911, notifies the Nurse Supervisor and Administrator at once and completes an incident report (see SAF-02).
The agency keeps all written transport approvals and reviews them at least annually. Transport incidents and safety training completion are reviewed in QAPI.

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME] who create, use, store or release client records, including the Administrator, Nurse Supervisors, CHHAs, schedulers and billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has a complete, accurate and secure record that shows the plan of care, delegation and services delivered, and that records are kept for the required time and available to those entitled to them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for every client. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9 (C9), the agency keeps the original plan of care and every revised plan, and gives copies to the patient or the patient's representative. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7 (C8), the supervisor documents in the patient's record every task delegated to a CHHA. Weekly activity records are retained with the medical record for at least seven years for adult clients and at least 21 years for pediatric clients, or longer if another law, a payer contract or a legal hold requires. Waivers of the 24-hour timing for giving the Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides are kept for at least two years (see ADM-13). Privacy documentation is retained as required by 45 CFR 164.530(j). Client records are confidential and are handled under ADM-10.

definitions.definition: The paper or electronic file that holds all documents about a client's services, including intake, assessments, plans of care, delegation records, supervisory contacts and visits, weekly activity records, incident reports, service agreement, consents and discharge documents.
A client under 18 years of age at the time of service.
The minimum time a record must be kept after the date of the last service or, for a minor, as stated in this policy and by law.
An instruction from the Administrator or counsel to keep records beyond the normal retention period because of a pending claim, audit, investigation or complaint.

procedures: The Nurse Supervisor opens a record for each client at intake (see CLN-01 and CLN-02). The record contains, at a minimum: intake documentation, in-person nursing assessment, signed plan of care, delegation records, service agreement and rate disclosure, Consumer Guide acknowledgment, consents, authorization documents (for Medicaid clients), and emergency plan.

The record also contains the weekly CHHA activity records, the 30-day supervisory contact notes, the 60-day in-person re-evaluation notes, nurse supervisor observation reports, incident reports concerning the client, communications with practitioners and payers, and the discharge or transfer summary (see CLN-07, CLN-08, CLN-09 and CLN-14).

The Nurse Supervisor files the original plan of care and every revised plan in the record, signed by the preparer with license designation, and records the date each copy was given to the patient or representative (see CLN-04).

The supervisor records in the patient record every task delegated to the CHHA, with the date, the task, and the supervisor's confirmation that the CHHA demonstrated competence. The delegation record is kept with the plan of care (see CLN-05).

Entries are made promptly, in ink or by electronic signature with date and time, and state facts. Errors are corrected by a single line and initials, or by an audit-trail amendment in the electronic system. Records are never altered to hide an entry.
Weekly activity records are collected from CHHAs each week, checked by the Nurse Supervisor, and filed with the medical record (see CLN-07).

The agency retains each client record, including weekly activity records, for at least seven years after the last date of service for adult clients. For a pediatric client, the record is retained for at least 21 years, or until the client reaches age 21 plus the retention period if longer, whichever the law requires. The Administrator extends retention when a payer contract, other law or a legal hold requires longer.

The Administrator keeps waivers of the 24-hour Consumer Guide timing for at least two years from the date of the waiver, in the client record or a waiver file that can be found by client name (see ADM-13).

The Administrator retains privacy policies, notices, authorizations, complaints, sanctions and training documentation required by 45 CFR 164.530(j) for at least six years from the date created or last in effect, whichever is later (see ADM-10).

Active records are kept in locked cabinets or in a password-protected electronic system with role-based access, audit trails and automatic log-off. Only staff with a need to know may see a record (see ADM-10).

Records are not removed from the office or system except as needed for care, and records carried in the field are kept secure. Lost or stolen records are reported to the Administrator immediately and handled as an incident (see SAF-02).

The client or representative may ask to review or get a copy of the record. The Nurse Supervisor refers the request to the Administrator, who responds within the time limits of HIPAA and other law, and logs the request and response.

The agency releases records to others only with a signed authorization or as the law allows. Surveyors from the Division of Consumer Affairs, payers, MCOs and other authorized reviewers are given access as required by law and contract. The Administrator logs each release.
Electronic records are backed up at least daily and stored securely off-site or in the cloud with a recovery test at least annually (see SAF-04).

Closed records are kept in an indexed file by client name and last service date. The Administrator reviews the closed-record file at least annually to find records that have passed their retention period and are not under a legal hold.

Records past their retention period are destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion, with a destruction log that records the date, method and person responsible. Records are never thrown away intact.

If [AGENCY NAME] closes, merges or is sold, the Administrator arranges for safe custody of all client records for the full retention period, tells clients how to get their records and reports as required (see REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Is the records custodian, enforces retention periods and legal holds, responds to access requests, approves destruction and ensures safe custody if the agency closes.

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, owners, officers, directors and principals, and the office staff of [AGENCY NAME] who prepare or file reports with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] files every report, financial statement and notice required to keep its Health Care Service Firm (HCSF) registration current and in good standing with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs (DCA), Regulated Business Section.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports to DCA on time and accurately. Written changes to application information are reported within 30 calendar days. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3 (C3), owner and managing-agent information is given before any change in ownership or management, and, if an officer, director, principal or owner is convicted after filing, a new affidavit is filed within 30 days of the conviction. Loss of accreditation is reported to DCA within 10 days. Under P.L. 2014, c.29 (C17), the agency obtains accreditation from a Department of Human Services-recognized accrediting body within 12 months of registration. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5 (C4), renewal includes evidence of accreditation and the financial statements and audits required under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A (C5). Under C5, the financial statement for the prior calendar year is due by July 1 each year, must match the firm's State tax filing, and is filed with the renewal. The Administrator confirms current filing requirements with DCA before each filing, because some audit and report requirements may be suspended or changed.

definitions.definition: The information in the HCSF registration, including firm and trade names, primary locations, officers, directors, principals, owners of 10% or more, managing agents, criminal-conviction certifications, bond or net-worth waiver documents, and the list of licenses held in other states with any actions taken.
Every day including weekends and holidays. The 30-day period starts on the day after the change occurs.
Accreditation from a New Jersey Department of Human Services-recognized accrediting body.
A statement for the prior calendar year showing assets, liabilities, gross income, operating expenses and money received for NJ Medicaid PCA services, which must match the firm's State tax filing.
The agency's tracking tool, kept by the Administrator, that lists each reporting event, the deadline, the responsible person and the date filed.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a reporting calendar listing the registration expiration date, the July 1 financial statement deadline, the accreditation 12-month deadline and renewal date, insurance and bond expiration dates, and each report due. The calendar is reviewed monthly, and key dates are set with reminders 90, 60 and 30 days in advance.

The Administrator confirms the current registration expiration date with DCA through the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal (https://rgbportal.dca.njoag.gov/), by phone at (973) 504-6370 or by email at regulatedbusiness@dca.njoag.gov. The Administrator notes that the annual expiration date has been changed by recent legislation from June 30 to September 30 and verifies how this applies to the agency.

Before any change in ownership or in managing agent, the Administrator provides DCA with the new owner and managing-agent information, using the Director-provided forms, so that DCA has it before the change takes effect (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3 (C3)). No change is finalized until the information has been submitted.

For any other change to application information, such as a name, address, officer, director, principal, phone or email, the Administrator reports it to DCA's Regulated Business Section in writing within 30 calendar days. The Administrator keeps a copy of the written notice and proof of delivery or portal confirmation.

Each officer, director, principal and owner must tell the Administrator immediately of any criminal charge or conviction. If one is convicted after the filing, the Administrator obtains a new criminal-conviction affidavit from that person and files it with DCA within 30 days of the conviction. The Administrator then reviews the person's role with the governing body and takes action as needed (see ADM-01 and ADM-06).

The Administrator tracks the bond and insurance requirements for registration: the $10,000 bond (or a waiver approved by the Director for a net worth of $100,000 or more, shown by a certified financial report) and the certificate of general professional liability insurance of at least $1,000,000. Any change or lapse is reported to DCA as an application change.

The Administrator ensures that the agency obtains accreditation from a DHS-recognized accrediting body within 12 months of the date of registration (P.L. 2014, c.29 (C17)). The Administrator chooses the body, schedules the survey early enough to meet the deadline and tracks each step on the reporting calendar (see ADM-05).

If the agency loses accreditation for any reason, the Administrator reports the loss to DCA in writing within 10 days of learning of it, keeps proof of filing, and starts a plan to regain accreditation. The Administrator also tells the governing body and any payers or MCOs that require notice (see ADM-05).

By July 1 each year, the Administrator files the financial statement for the prior calendar year with DCA. The statement is prepared by the agency's accountant, shows assets, liabilities, gross income, operating expenses and money received for NJ Medicaid PCA services, and matches the firm's State tax filing (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A (C5)).

The Administrator and the accountant determine whether an audit or CPA-reviewed report is needed, by looking at NJ Medicaid PCA revenue and gross income: an audit for more than $250,000 in NJ Medicaid PCA revenue or $10 million or more in gross income, and a report with a review by a NJ-licensed CPA for less than $250,000 in PCA revenue and $1 million to under $10 million in gross income. Audits must have an unqualified opinion with compliance and financial components. Before filing, the Administrator confirms with DCA whether these requirements are currently in force or suspended, and records the answer.

At renewal, the Administrator submits through the portal the renewal application, the annual registration fee for each primary location, evidence of current accreditation (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5 (C4)), the financial statements and audits required by C5, and any updated insurance, bond, ownership and conviction-certification documents.

The Administrator submits the renewal before the expiration date, at least 30 days ahead when possible, and checks the portal to confirm the renewal has been processed. The agency does not place CHHAs with clients after the registration expires. If DCA has not confirmed renewal by the expiration date, the Administrator contacts DCA the same day and tells the governing body.

Reports that relate to client or caregiver events, such as abuse, neglect or exploitation, are handled under SAF-01, SAF-02 and ADM-06. Reports to payers, MCOs and the Personal Preference Program are handled under MED-03.

All reports, notices, portal confirmations, fees, certified financial reports, audits and DCA correspondence are filed in a regulatory file kept by the Administrator and are retained for at least seven years. They are available to the governing body and to surveyors.

The Administrator reports the status of all filings to the governing body at least quarterly and to the QAPI Committee as part of the compliance review (see ADM-14). Any late or missed report is treated as a compliance incident, and a corrective action plan is recorded.

required_items.text: A Nurse Supervisor conducts an in-person re-evaluation every 60 days (or 2 months), or more often if the patient's condition warrants. More frequent re-evaluation also applies after an interruption of service, a hospitalization or facility stay, or a change in condition or functional status, or if consistent with a service agreement.
required_items.cite: Best Practices §II, Periodic Patient Review and Re-Evaluation

required_items.text: If the nurse changes the plan of care, the documentation reflects the reasons, based on review of: (1) nursing and medical diagnosis(es) or problem(s); (2) changes in vital signs, including temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure and a pain assessment; (3) changes in functional status; (4) psycho-social review relevant to the Plan of Care; (5) nutritional status, including diet; (6) home safety review, including fall risk assessment; (7) the emergency plan.

Provide an orientation program quarterly to all newly hired CHHAs within three months of employment, or sooner based on the CHHA's documented level of expertise.

Orientation covers at minimum: (1) infection control; (2) blood-borne pathogens; (3) child abuse; (4) elder abuse; (5) domestic violence; (6) pain management; (7) patient rights; (8) HIPAA; (9) corporate compliance; (10) ethical considerations in home care delivery, including receipt of gifts and money from clients and other financial transactions; (11) employee safety; (12) emergency procedures; (13) agency administrative and clinical policies and procedures.

Orientation documentation includes: (1) outline of topics covered; (2) length of time for each of the mandatory in-service topics; (3) date and signature of instructor; (4) name, date and signature of employees on an agency sign-in sheet. Attendance records are maintained and may be electronic if readily retrievable and printable.

Provide an in-service program at least once each year (or over the course of a year) for all CHHAs, covering at minimum: (1) blood-borne pathogens; (2) infection control; (3) standard precautions; (4) child abuse; (5) elder abuse; (6) domestic violence; (7) pain management; (8) workforce protection; (9) employee safety issues; (10) back safety; (11) how to handle needle sticks; (12) fraud and abuse prevention; (13) corporate compliance. An HCSF may accept another HCSF's documentation that a CHHA met some or all of these topics. Attendance records are maintained.

All CHHAs undergo clinical competency testing by a Nurse Supervisor before or on the first date of assignment. This includes direct observation of delegated personal care services related to: (a) the musculo-skeletal system; (b) the integumentary system; (c) the upper and lower gastrointestinal system; (d) the urinary system; (e) the cardiovascular and respiratory systems (vital signs, antiembolic stockings, oxygen assistance, positioning); (f) the neurological system (cognitive impairment, seizure disorder, post-stroke care, rehabilitation or restorative care); (g) the endocrine system (foot care, skin care and nutrition for a client with diabetes); (h) the promotion of sleep. If direct observation is impractical or intrusive, the Nurse Supervisor may ask the CHHA to describe how the task would be performed.
required_items.cite: Best Practices §III, Clinical Competency: Prior to or on the date of the first Assignment, 1(a)-(h)

required_items.text: Written testing, oral testing or direct observation of the CHHA's knowledge and communication skills in: (a) observation, reporting and documentation of patient status and care furnished; (b) basic infection control procedures; (c) basic elements of body mechanics and functioning, and changes in body function that must be reported to the Nurse Supervisor; (d) maintenance of a clean, safe and healthy environment; (e) recognizing emergencies and knowledge of emergency procedures; (f) physical, emotional and developmental needs of and ways to work with the populations served, including respect for the patient and the patient's privacy and property; (g) adequate nutrition and fluid intake.

required_items.text: Competency documentation in the employee file includes: (1) name of the CHHA; (2) clinical skills tested, and the date and location of testing; (3) an evaluation of the CHHA's competency; (4) date and signature of the Nurse Supervisor performing the testing. At minimum, an assessment of competency is recorded by the end of each year of employment. Records may be electronic.

Patients and family/significant others are provided with full and truthful disclosure of all information concerning fees and billing policies.

Every certified homemaker-home health aide or health care professional regulated by the Division wears an identification tag at all times while providing care. The tag shows first name or initial, full surname, the term for the level of licensure or certification, and a photograph. Letters are of equal size, no smaller than one-quarter inch, and the tag is at least as large as any other identification worn.
Every health care service firm provides patient/employers with a copy of the Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides published by the NJ Board of Nursing.
The Consumer Guide is provided at least 24 hours before services are provided.
A patient/employer may waive the 24-hour timing in writing. The firm keeps the waiver for at least two years and still provides the information before services begin.
To place certified homemaker-home health aides, an agency regulated by the Division must be licensed as a health care service firm.
A health care service firm only refers or places actively certified homemaker-home health aides who are employed by the agency.
A homemaker-home health aide employed by an HCSF only performs tasks delegated by, or directed by, the health care practitioner supervisor.
The health care practitioner supervisor ensures the aide demonstrates competence to perform the client care that is delegated.
The health care practitioner supervisor documents in the patient's record every task delegated to a homemaker-home health aide.

Prohibited acts: (1) recruiting, advertising or contracting for health care services without first obtaining registration; (2) charging a fee or liquidated damages to employees (this requires an employment agency license under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-2); (3) preventing employees by contract from working for others (the same licensing consequence applies if a fee is charged); (4) knowingly sending staff to a facility where a strike or lockout is in progress, to replace strikers.

official.notes: No single official Division checklist or form lists the written policies for an HCSF. The binding rules (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3 and 13.5) cover only application paperwork, which was excluded. The Division's FAQ (HCSF-FAQ-07242025.pdf) also lists only application items: registration form, fee, formation documents, criminal-history certifications, $1M liability insurance, bond, practitioner-supervisor designation, and out-of-state licenses. The only official source that enumerates policy content is the Division's advisory 'Best Practices for Health Care Service Firms' (April 15, 2014). It says it is non-binding and that the statute and rules control, even where it uses 'shall'. Organize the manual in its order: II Clinical, III Personnel, IV Administrative, with the binding rule items (13:45B-13.6, 13.7, 14.7) cross-referenced in the matching policies. Registration is submitted online through the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal, and policies are not part of that submission. Keep the manual available for the Division's inspection and for the accrediting body, since HCSFs must obtain DHS-recognized accreditation within 12 months of registration. I did not fetch the NJ DHS-recognized accreditation standards or the Medicaid (PCA, MLTSS, PPP) manuals, so any added requirements from those sources are not captured here. Registration timing and financial reporting are in flux under P.L. 2026, c.45, and the Division says rule updates are pending. The 13:45B-13.3, 13:45B-14.7, 13:45B-13.6 and 13:45B-13.7 text came from Cornell LII mirrors, not the NJ Administrative Code directly. The Division's Subchapter 14 PDF could not be fetched. The Best Practices item IDs use my own section/heading plus the document's list number, because the document numbers each list separately and has no global item numbers.
